id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Nonetheless, the <i>Letter of Aristeas</i> is very late and contains information that is now known to be inaccurate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETracy2000343_24-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETracy2000343-24"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to <a href="/wiki/Diogenes_Laertius" title="Diogenes Laertius">Diogenes Laertius</a>, Demetrius was a student of <a href="/wiki/Theophrastus" title="Theophrastus">Theophrastus</a>, a student of Aristotle.<sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Other sources claim that the Library was instead created under the reign of Ptolemy I's son <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy_II_Philadelphus" title="Ptolemy II Philadelphus">Ptolemy II Philadelphus</a> (283–246 BC).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Modern scholars agree that, while it is possible that Ptolemy I, who was a historian and author<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200132_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200132-27"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> of an account of Alexander's campaign, may have laid the groundwork for the Library, it probably did not come into being as a physical institution until the reign of Ptolemy II.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETracy2000343_24-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETracy2000343-24"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> By that time, Demetrius of Phalerum had fallen out of favor with the Ptolemaic court. He probably would not, therefore, have had any role in establishing the Library as an institution.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETracy2000343–344_2-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETracy2000343–344-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Stephen_V._Tracy" title="Stephen V. Tracy">Stephen V. Tracy</a>, however, argues that it is highly probable that Demetrius played an important role in collecting at least some of the earliest texts that would later become part of the Library's collection.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETracy2000343–344_2-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETracy2000343–344-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In around 295 BC, Demetrius may have acquired early texts of the writings of Aristotle and <a href="/wiki/Theophrastus" title="Theophrastus">Theophrastus</a>, which he would have been uniquely positioned to do since he was a distinguished member of the Peripatetic school.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETracy2000344–345_28-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETracy2000344–345-28"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>28<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The Library was built in the Brucheion (Royal Quarter) as part of the <a href="/wiki/Mouseion" title="Mouseion">Mouseion</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWiegandDavis201519_29-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWiegandDavis201519-29"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>a<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Its main purpose was to show off the wealth of Egypt, with research as a lesser goal,<sup id="cite_ref-Lindberg1980_23-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Lindberg1980-23"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> but its contents were used to aid the ruler of Egypt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20001–_32-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20001–-32"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The exact layout of the library is not known, but ancient sources describe the Library of Alexandria as comprising a collection of scrolls, Greek columns, a <i lang="en"><a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Peripatetic#English" class="extiw" title="wikt:Peripatetic">peripatos</a></i> walk, a room for shared dining, a reading room, meeting rooms, gardens, and lecture halls, creating a model for the modern university campus.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELyons201126_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELyons201126-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A hall contained shelves for the collections of papyrus scrolls known as <i>bibliothekai</i> (<i>βιβλιοθῆκαι</i>). According to popular description, an inscription above the shelves read: "The place of the cure of the soul."<sup id="cite_ref-Alberto2008_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Alberto2008-34"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Early_expansion_and_organization">Early expansion and organization</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Early expansion and organization"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Antikes_Alexandria_Karte.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Antikes_Alexandria_Karte.JPG/500px-Antikes_Alexandria_Karte.JPG" decoding="async" width="500" height="388" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.5" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Antikes_Alexandria_Karte.JPG/960px-Antikes_Alexandria_Karte.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1694" data-file-height="1314"></a><figcaption>Map of ancient Alexandria. The Mouseion was located in the royal Broucheion quarter (listed on this map as "Bruchium") in the central part of the city near the Great Harbor ("Portus Magnus" on the map).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBarnes200062_35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes200062-35"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>The Ptolemaic rulers intended the Library to be a collection of all knowledge<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20001–_32-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20001–-32"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and they worked to expand the Library's collections through an aggressive and well-funded policy of book purchasing.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200134_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200134-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> They dispatched royal agents with large amounts of money and ordered them to purchase and collect as many texts as they possibly could, about any subject and by any author.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200134_36-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200134-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Older copies of texts were favored over newer ones, since it was assumed that older copies had undergone less copying and that they were therefore more likely to more closely resemble what the original author had written.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200134_36-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200134-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This program involved trips to the book fairs of <a href="/wiki/Rhodes" title="Rhodes">Rhodes</a> and <a href="/wiki/Athens" title="Athens">Athens</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to the Greek medical writer <a href="/wiki/Galen" title="Galen">Galen</a>, under the decree of Ptolemy II, any books found on ships that came into port were taken to the library, where they were copied by official scribes.<sup id="cite_ref-Galen_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Galen-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004–5_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004–5-39"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFox1986341_19-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox1986341-19"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The original texts were kept in the library, and the copies delivered to the owners.<sup id="cite_ref-Galen_38-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Galen-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFox1986341_19-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox1986341-19"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Library particularly focused on acquiring manuscripts of the Homeric poems, which were the foundation of Greek education and revered above all other poems.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200136_40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200136-40"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Library therefore acquired many different manuscripts of these poems, tagging each copy with a label to indicate where it had come from.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200136_40-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200136-40"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In addition to collecting works from the past, the Mouseion which housed the Library also served as home to a host of international scholars, poets, philosophers, and researchers, who, according to the first-century BC Greek geographer <a href="/wiki/Strabo" title="Strabo">Strabo</a>, were provided with a large salary, free food and lodging, and exemption from taxes.<sup id="cite_ref-Kennedy1999_41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Kennedy1999-41"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200133–34_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200133–34-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> They had a large, circular dining hall with a high domed ceiling in which they ate meals communally.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> There were also numerous classrooms, where the scholars were expected to at least occasionally teach students.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ptolemy II Philadelphus is said to have had a keen interest in zoology, so it has been speculated that the Mouseion may have even had a zoo for exotic animals.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to classical scholar <a href="/wiki/Lionel_Casson" title="Lionel Casson">Lionel Casson</a>, the idea was that if the scholars were completely freed from all the burdens of everyday life they would be able to devote more time to research and intellectual pursuits.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200134_36-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200134-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Strabo called the group of scholars who lived at the Mouseion a <a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%CF%83%CF%8D%CE%BD%CE%BF%CE%B4%CE%BF%CF%82" class="extiw" title="wikt:σύνοδος">σύνοδος</a> (<span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><i lang="grc-Latn">synodos</i></span>, "community").<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As early as 283 BC, they may have numbered between thirty and fifty learned men.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Early_scholarship">Early scholarship</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Early scholarship"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The Library of Alexandria was not affiliated with any particular philosophical school; consequently, scholars who studied there had considerable academic freedom.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> They were, however, subject to the authority of the king.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> One likely apocryphal story is told of a poet named <a href="/wiki/Sotades" title="Sotades">Sotades</a> who wrote an obscene epigram making fun of Ptolemy II for marrying his sister <a href="/wiki/Arsinoe_II" title="Arsinoe II">Arsinoe II</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ptolemy II is said to have jailed him and, after he escaped and was caught again, sealed him in a lead jar and dropped him into the sea.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As a religious center, the Mouseion was directed by a priest of the Muses known as an <i>epistates</i>, who was appointed by the king in the same manner as the priests who managed the various <a href="/wiki/Egyptian_temples" class="mw-redirect" title="Egyptian temples">Egyptian temples</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20003–4_44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20003–4-44"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Library itself was directed by a scholar who served as <a href="/wiki/Category:Librarians_of_Alexandria" title="Category:Librarians of Alexandria">head librarian</a>, as well as tutor to the king's son.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEStaikos200066_45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStaikos200066-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200137_47-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200137-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The first recorded head librarian was <a href="/wiki/Zenodotus_of_Ephesus" class="mw-redirect" title="Zenodotus of Ephesus">Zenodotus of Ephesus</a> (lived <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 325</span> – c.<span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 270 BC</span>).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200137_47-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200137-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Zenodotus' main work was devoted to the establishment of canonical texts for the Homeric poems and the early Greek lyric poets.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200137_47-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200137-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Most of what is known about him comes from later commentaries that mention his preferred readings of particular passages.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Zenodotus is known to have written a glossary of rare and unusual words, which was organized in <a href="/wiki/Alphabetical_order" title="Alphabetical order">alphabetical order</a>, making him the first person known to have employed alphabetical order as a method of organization.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200137_47-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200137-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Since the collection at the Library of Alexandria seems to have been organized in alphabetical order by the first letter of the author's name from very early, Casson concludes that it is highly probable that Zenodotus was the one who organized it in this way.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200137_47-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200137-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Zenodotus' system of alphabetization, however, only used the first letter of the word<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200137_47-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200137-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and it was not until the second century AD that anyone is known to have applied the same method of alphabetization to the remaining letters of the word.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200137_47-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200137-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Meanwhile, the scholar and poet <a href="/wiki/Callimachus" title="Callimachus">Callimachus</a> compiled the <i><a href="/wiki/Pinakes" title="Pinakes">Pinakes</a></i>, a 120-book catalogue of various authors and all their known works.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEStaikos200066_45-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStaikos200066-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <i>Pinakes</i> has not survived, but enough references to it and fragments of it have survived to allow scholars to reconstruct its basic structure.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200139–40_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200139–40-48"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <i>Pinakes</i> was divided into multiple sections, each containing entries for writers of a particular genre of literature.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200139–40_48-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200139–40-48"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The most basic division was between writers of poetry and prose, with each section divided into smaller subsections.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200139–40_48-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200139–40-48"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Each section listed authors in alphabetical order.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200140_49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200140-49"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Each entry included the author's name, father's name, place of birth, and other brief biographical information, sometimes including nicknames by which that author was known, followed by a complete list of all that author's known works.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200140_49-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200140-49"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The entries for prolific authors such as <a href="/wiki/Aeschylus" title="Aeschylus">Aeschylus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Euripides" title="Euripides">Euripides</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sophocles" title="Sophocles">Sophocles</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Theophrastus" title="Theophrastus">Theophrastus</a> must have been extremely long, spanning multiple columns of text.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200140_49-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200140-49"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Although Callimachus did his most famous work at the Library of Alexandria, he never held the position of head librarian there.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEStaikos200066_45-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStaikos200066-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Callimachus' pupil <a href="/wiki/Hermippus_of_Smyrna" title="Hermippus of Smyrna">Hermippus of Smyrna</a> wrote biographies, <a href="/wiki/Philostephanus_of_Cyrene" class="mw-redirect" title="Philostephanus of Cyrene">Philostephanus of Cyrene</a> studied geography, and <a href="/wiki/Istros_the_Callimachean" title="Istros the Callimachean">Istros</a> (who may have also been from Cyrene) studied Attic antiquities.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015109_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015109-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In addition to the Great Library, many other smaller libraries also began to spring up all around the city of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Archimedes-screw_one-screw-threads_with-ball_3D-view_animated_small.gif" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Archimedes-screw_one-screw-threads_with-ball_3D-view_animated_small.gif/250px-Archimedes-screw_one-screw-threads_with-ball_3D-view_animated_small.gif" decoding="async" width="250" height="181" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Archimedes-screw_one-screw-threads_with-ball_3D-view_animated_small.gif/500px-Archimedes-screw_one-screw-threads_with-ball_3D-view_animated_small.gif 2x" data-file-width="505" data-file-height="365"></a><figcaption>According to legend, the Syracusan inventor <a href="/wiki/Archimedes" title="Archimedes">Archimedes</a> invented the <a href="/wiki/Archimedes%27_screw" title="Archimedes' screw">Archimedes' screw</a>, a pump for transporting water, while studying at the Library of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006_51-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>After Zenodotus either died or retired, Ptolemy II Philadelphus appointed <a href="/wiki/Apollonius_of_Rhodes" title="Apollonius of Rhodes">Apollonius of Rhodes</a> (lived <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 295</span> – c.<span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 215 BC</span>), a native of Alexandria and a student of Callimachus, as the second head librarian of the Library of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015109_50-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015109-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006_51-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Philadelphus also appointed Apollonius of Rhodes as the tutor to his son, the future <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy_III_Euergetes" title="Ptolemy III Euergetes">Ptolemy III Euergetes</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015109_50-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015109-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Apollonius of Rhodes is best known as the author of the <i><a href="/wiki/Argonautica" title="Argonautica">Argonautica</a></i>, an epic poem about the voyages of <a href="/wiki/Jason" title="Jason">Jason</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Argonauts" title="Argonauts">Argonauts</a>, which has survived to the present in its complete form.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015110_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015110-52"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006_51-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <i>Argonautica</i> displays Apollonius' vast knowledge of history and literature and makes allusions to a vast array of events and texts while simultaneously imitating the style of the Homeric poems.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015110_52-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015110-52"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Some fragments of his scholarly writings have also survived, but he is generally more famous today as a poet than as a scholar.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>According to legend, during the librarianship of Apollonius, the mathematician and inventor <a href="/wiki/Archimedes" title="Archimedes">Archimedes</a> (lived <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 287 – <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 212 BC) came to visit the Library of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006_51-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During his time in Egypt, Archimedes is said to have observed the rise and fall of the <a href="/wiki/Nile" title="Nile">Nile</a>, leading him to invent the <a href="/wiki/Archimedes%27_screw" title="Archimedes' screw">Archimedes' screw</a>, which can be used to transport water from low-lying bodies into irrigation ditches.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006_51-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Archimedes later returned to Syracuse, where he continued making new inventions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006_51-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>According to two late and largely unreliable biographies, Apollonius was forced to resign from his position as head librarian and moved to the island of Rhodes (after which he takes his name) on account of the hostile reception he received in Alexandria to the first draft of his <i>Argonautica</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015109–110_53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015109–110-53"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It is more likely that Apollonius' resignation was on account of Ptolemy III Euergetes' ascension to the throne in 246 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015110_52-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015110-52"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Later_scholarship_and_expansion">Later scholarship and expansion</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Later scholarship and expansion"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The third head librarian, <a href="/wiki/Eratosthenes_of_Cyrene" class="mw-redirect" title="Eratosthenes of Cyrene">Eratosthenes of Cyrene</a> (lived <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 280–<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 194 BC), is best known today for his scientific works, but he was also a literary scholar.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEStaikos200066_45-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStaikos200066-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015114_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015114-54"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006_51-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Eratosthenes' most important work was his treatise <i>Geographika</i>, which was originally in three volumes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015115_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015115-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The work itself has not survived, but many fragments of it are preserved through quotation in the writings of the later geographer <a href="/wiki/Strabo" title="Strabo">Strabo</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015115_55-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015115-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Eratosthenes was the first scholar to apply mathematics to geography and map-making<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015116_56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015116-56"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and, in his treatise <i>Concerning the Measurement of the Earth</i>, he calculated the circumference of the earth and was only off by less than a few hundred kilometers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015116_56-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015116-56"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006_51-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200141_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200141-57"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Eratosthenes also produced a map of the entire known world, which incorporated information taken from sources held in the Library, including accounts of <a href="/wiki/Indian_campaign_of_Alexander_the_Great" title="Indian campaign of Alexander the Great">Alexander the Great's campaigns in India</a> and reports written by members of Ptolemaic elephant-hunting expeditions along the coast of East Africa.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200141_57-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200141-57"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Eratosthenes was the first person to advance geography towards becoming a scientific discipline.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015116–117_58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015116–117-58"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Eratosthenes believed that the setting of the Homeric poems was purely imaginary and argued that the purpose of poetry was "to capture the soul", rather than to give a historically accurate account of actual events.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015115_55-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015115-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Strabo quotes him as having sarcastically commented, "a man might find the places of Odysseus' wanderings if the day were to come when he would find the leatherworker who stitched the goatskin of the winds."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015115_55-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015115-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Meanwhile, scholars at the Library of Alexandria displayed interest in other scientific subjects.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006–7_60-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20006–7-60"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Bacchius_of_Tanagra" title="Bacchius of Tanagra">Bacchius of Tanagra</a>, a contemporary of Eratosthenes, edited and commented on the medical writings of the <a href="/wiki/Hippocratic_Corpus" title="Hippocratic Corpus">Hippocratic Corpus</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117_59-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The doctors <a href="/wiki/Herophilos" title="Herophilos">Herophilus</a> (lived <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 335–<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 280 BC) and <a href="/wiki/Erasistratus" title="Erasistratus">Erasistratus</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 304–<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 250 BC) studied <a href="/wiki/Human_anatomy" title="Human anatomy">human anatomy</a>, but their studies were hindered by protests against the <a href="/wiki/Dissection" title="Dissection">dissection</a> of human corpses, which was seen as immoral.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007_61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>According to Galen, around this time, Ptolemy III requested permission from the Athenians to borrow the original manuscripts of <a href="/wiki/Aeschylus" title="Aeschylus">Aeschylus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sophocles" title="Sophocles">Sophocles</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Euripides" title="Euripides">Euripides</a>, for which the Athenians demanded the enormous amount of fifteen <a href="/wiki/Talent_(measurement)" title="Talent (measurement)">talents</a> (1,000 lb; 450 kg) of a precious metal as guarantee that he would return them.<sup id="cite_ref-Galenxviia_62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Galenxviia-62"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200135_5-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200135-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013147–148_63-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013147–148-63"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ptolemy III had expensive copies of the plays made on the highest quality papyrus and sent the Athenians the copies, keeping the original manuscripts for the library<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and telling the Athenians they could keep the talents.<sup id="cite_ref-Galenxviia_62-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Galenxviia-62"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004_43-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20004-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200135_5-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200135-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013147–148_63-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013147–148-63"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This story may also be construed to show the power of Alexandria over Athens during the <a href="/wiki/Ptolemaic_dynasty" title="Ptolemaic dynasty">Ptolemaic dynasty</a>. This detail arises from the fact that Alexandria was a man-made bidirectional port between the mainland and the <a href="/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria" title="Lighthouse of Alexandria">Pharos</a> island, welcoming trade from the East and West, and soon found itself to be an international hub for trade, the leading producer of papyrus and, soon enough, books.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETrumbleMacIntyre_Marshall2003_64-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrumbleMacIntyre_Marshall2003-64"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As the Library expanded, it ran out of space to house the scrolls in its collection, so, during the reign of Ptolemy III Euergetes, it opened a satellite collection in the <a href="/wiki/Serapeum_of_Alexandria" title="Serapeum of Alexandria">Serapeum of Alexandria</a>, a temple to the Greco-Egyptian god <a href="/wiki/Serapis" title="Serapis">Serapis</a> located near the royal palace.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200134_36-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200134-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Peak_of_literary_criticism">Peak of literary criticism</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Peak of literary criticism"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Alexandria_-_Pompey%27s_Pillar_-_view_of_ruins.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Alexandria_-_Pompey%27s_Pillar_-_view_of_ruins.JPG/250px-Alexandria_-_Pompey%27s_Pillar_-_view_of_ruins.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Alexandria_-_Pompey%27s_Pillar_-_view_of_ruins.JPG/500px-Alexandria_-_Pompey%27s_Pillar_-_view_of_ruins.JPG 2x" data-file-width="3264" data-file-height="2448"></a><figcaption>Present-day ruins of the <a href="/wiki/Serapeum_of_Alexandria" title="Serapeum of Alexandria">Serapeum of Alexandria</a>, where the Library of Alexandria moved part of its collection after it ran out of storage space in the main building<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005_9-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20005-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Aristophanes_of_Byzantium" title="Aristophanes of Byzantium">Aristophanes of Byzantium</a> (lived <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 257–<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 180 BC) became the fourth head librarian sometime around 200 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200138_65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200138-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to a legend recorded by the Roman writer <a href="/wiki/Vitruvius" title="Vitruvius">Vitruvius</a>, Aristophanes was one of seven judges appointed for a poetry competition hosted by Ptolemy III Euergetes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200138_65-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200138-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013148–149_66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013148–149-66"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> All six of the other judges favored one competitor, but Aristophanes favored the one whom the audience had liked the least.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200138_65-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200138-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149_67-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Aristophanes declared that all of the poets except for the one he had chosen had committed plagiarism and were therefore disqualified.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200138_65-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200138-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149_67-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The king demanded that he prove this, so he retrieved the texts that the authors had plagiarized from the Library, locating them by memory.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200138_65-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200138-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149_67-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On account of his impressive memory and diligence, Ptolemy III appointed him as head librarian.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149_67-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The librarianship of Aristophanes of Byzantium is widely considered to have opened a more mature phase of scholarship in the Library of Alexandria's history.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015118_68-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015118-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007_61-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During this phase, <a href="/wiki/Literary_criticism" title="Literary criticism">literary criticism</a> reached its peak<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015118_68-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015118-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and came to dominate the Library's scholarly output.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007–8_69-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007–8-69"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Aristophanes of Byzantium edited poetic texts and introduced the division of poems into separate lines on the page, since they had previously been written out just like prose.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075,_93_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075,_93-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He also invented the system of <a href="/wiki/Greek_diacritics" title="Greek diacritics">Greek diacritics</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075,_92–93_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075,_92–93-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007_61-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> wrote important works on <a href="/wiki/Lexicography" title="Lexicography">lexicography</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and introduced a series of signs for textual criticism.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey200793_72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey200793-72"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He wrote introductions to many plays, some of which have survived in partially rewritten forms.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The fifth head librarian was an obscure individual named <a href="/wiki/Apollonius_Eidographus" title="Apollonius Eidographus">Apollonius Eidographus</a>, who is known by the epithet "the classifier of forms" (<a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Ancient Greek language">Ancient Greek</a>: <span lang="grc">ὁ εἰδογράφος</span>).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015129_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015129-73"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> One late lexicographical source explains this epithet as referring to the classification of poetry on the basis of musical forms.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015129_73-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015129-73"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>During the early second century BC, several scholars at the Library of Alexandria studied works on medicine.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117_59-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Zeuxis the Empiricist is credited with having written commentaries on the Hippocratic Corpus,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117_59-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and he actively worked to procure medical writings for the Library's collection.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117_59-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A scholar named Ptolemy Epithetes wrote a treatise on wounds in the Homeric poems, a subject straddling the line between traditional philology and medicine.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117_59-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015117-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> However, it was also during the early second century BC that the political power of Ptolemaic Egypt began to decline.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173_74-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Raphia" title="Battle of Raphia">Battle of Raphia</a> in 217 BC, Ptolemaic power became increasingly unstable.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173_74-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> There were uprisings among segments of the Egyptian population and, in the first half of the second century BC, connection with <a href="/wiki/Upper_Egypt" title="Upper Egypt">Upper Egypt</a> became largely disrupted.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173_74-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ptolemaic rulers also began to emphasize the Egyptian aspect of their nation over the Greek aspect.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173_74-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Consequently, many Greek scholars began to leave Alexandria for safer countries with more generous patronages.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173_74-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Aristarchus_of_Samothrace" title="Aristarchus of Samothrace">Aristarchus of Samothrace</a> (lived <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 216–<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 145 BC) was the sixth head librarian.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He earned a reputation as the greatest of all ancient scholars of Homeric poetry and produced not only texts of classic poems and works of prose, but full <i><a href="/wiki/Hypomnema" title="Hypomnema">hypomnemata</a></i>, or long, free-standing commentaries, on them.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> These commentaries would typically cite a passage of a classical text, explain its meaning, define any unusual words used in it, and comment on whether the words in the passage were really those used by the original author or if they were later interpolations added by scribes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200143_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200143-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He made many contributions to a variety of studies, but particularly the study of the Homeric poems,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and his editorial opinions are widely quoted by ancient authors as authoritative.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A portion of one of Aristarchus' commentaries on the <i><a href="/wiki/Histories_(Herodotus)" title="Histories (Herodotus)">Histories</a></i> of <a href="/wiki/Herodotus" title="Herodotus">Herodotus</a> has survived in a papyrus fragment.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200143_75-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200143-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 145 BC, however, Aristarchus became caught up in a dynastic struggle in which he supported <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy_VII_Neos_Philopator" title="Ptolemy VII Neos Philopator">Ptolemy VII Neos Philopator</a> as the ruler of Egypt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015130_76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015130-76"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ptolemy VII was murdered and succeeded by <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy_VIII_Physcon" title="Ptolemy VIII Physcon">Ptolemy VIII Physcon</a>, who immediately set about punishing all those who had supported his predecessor, forcing Aristarchus to flee Egypt and take refuge on the island of <a href="/wiki/Cyprus" title="Cyprus">Cyprus</a>, where he died shortly after.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMontana2015130_76-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMontana2015130-76"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ptolemy VIII expelled all foreign scholars from Alexandria, forcing them to disperse across the Eastern Mediterranean.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075_46-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173_74-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995173-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Decline">Decline</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Decline"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="After_Ptolemy_VIII's_expulsions"><span id="After_Ptolemy_VIII.27s_expulsions"></span>After Ptolemy VIII's expulsions</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: After Ptolemy VIII's expulsions"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Ptolemy VIII Physcon's expulsion of the scholars from Alexandria brought about a shift in the history of Hellenistic scholarship.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075–6_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075–6-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The scholars who had studied at the Library of Alexandria and their students continued to conduct research and write treatises, but most of them no longer did so in association with the Library.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075–6_77-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075–6-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Due to this, the Library of Alexandria began to decline in respect and prestige.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A <a href="/wiki/Diaspora" title="Diaspora">diaspora</a> of Alexandrian scholarship occurred, in which scholars of the Library dispersed first into the eastern Mediterranean and then into the world of the western Mediterranean as well.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20075–6_77-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20075–6-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Former scholars and their disciples took their scholarly energies elsewhere. For example, Aristarchus' student <a href="/wiki/Dionysius_Thrax" title="Dionysius Thrax">Dionysius Thrax</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 170</span> – c.<span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 90 BC</span>) established a school on the Greek island of Rhodes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20076_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20076-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200145_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200145-79"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He also wrote the <a href="/wiki/The_Art_of_Grammar" title="The Art of Grammar">first book on Greek grammar</a>, a succinct guide to speaking and writing clearly and effectively<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200145_79-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200145-79"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> – a book that remained the primary grammar textbook for Greek schoolboys until as late as the twelfth century AD.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200145_79-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200145-79"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Another one of Aristarchus' pupils, <a href="/wiki/Apollodorus_of_Athens" title="Apollodorus of Athens">Apollodorus of Athens</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 180</span> – c.<span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 110 BC</span>), went to Alexandria's greatest rival, Pergamum, where he taught and conducted research.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20076_78-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20076-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This scholarly diaspora prompted the historian <a href="/wiki/Menecles_of_Barca" title="Menecles of Barca">Menecles of Barca</a> to sarcastically comment that Alexandria had become the teacher of all Greeks and barbarians alike.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995373_80-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeyboom1995373-80"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Meanwhile, in Alexandria, from the middle of the second century BC onwards, Ptolemaic rule in Egypt grew less stable than it had been previously.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Confronted with growing social unrest and other major political and economic problems, the later Ptolemies did not devote as much attention towards the Library and the Mouseion as their predecessors had, continuing the decline that had begun under Ptolemy VIII Physcon.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The status of both the Library and the head librarian diminished.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Several of the later Ptolemies used the position of head librarian as a mere political plum to reward their most devoted supporters.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ptolemy VIII appointed a man named Cydas, one of his palace guards, as head librarian<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy_IX_Lathyros" class="mw-redirect" title="Ptolemy IX Lathyros">Ptolemy IX Soter II</a> (ruled 88–81 BC) is said to have given the position to a political supporter.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Eventually, the position of head librarian lost so much of its former prestige that even contemporary authors ceased to take interest in recording the terms of office for individual head librarians.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>A shift in Greek scholarship at large occurred around the beginning of the first century BC.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20076_78-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20076-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFox1986351_83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox1986351-83"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> By this time, all major classical poetic texts had finally been standardized and extensive commentaries had already been produced on the writings of all the major literary authors of the <a href="/wiki/Greek_Classical_Era" class="mw-redirect" title="Greek Classical Era">Greek Classical Era</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20076_78-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20076-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Consequently, there was little original work left for scholars to do with these texts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20076_78-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20076-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Many scholars began producing syntheses and reworkings of the commentaries of the Alexandrian scholars of previous centuries, at the expense of their own originalities.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20076_78-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20076-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFox1986351_83-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox1986351-83"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>b<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Other scholars branched out and began writing commentaries on the poetic works of postclassical authors, including Alexandrian poets such as Callimachus and Apollonius of Rhodes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20076_78-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20076-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Meanwhile, Alexandrian scholarship was probably introduced to <a href="/wiki/Rome" title="Rome">Rome</a> in the first century BC by <a href="/wiki/Tyrannion_of_Amisus" title="Tyrannion of Amisus">Tyrannion of Amisus</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 100</span> – c.<span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 25 BC</span>), a student of Dionysius Thrax.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20076_78-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20076-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Burning_by_Julius_Caesar">Burning by Julius Caesar</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Burning by Julius Caesar"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:C%C3%A9sar_(13667960455).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/C%C3%A9sar_%2813667960455%29.jpg/250px-C%C3%A9sar_%2813667960455%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="380" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.75" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/C%C3%A9sar_%2813667960455%29.jpg/500px-C%C3%A9sar_%2813667960455%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1117" data-file-height="1698"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Julius_Caesar" title="Julius Caesar">Julius Caesar</a> burned his ships during the <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Alexandria_(47_BC)" title="Siege of Alexandria (47 BC)">Siege of Alexandria</a> in 48 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ancient writers said the fire spread and destroyed part of the Library's collections;<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> the Library seems to have partially survived or been quickly rebuilt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>In 48 BC, during <a href="/wiki/Caesar%27s_Civil_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Caesar's Civil War">Caesar's Civil War</a>, <a href="/wiki/Julius_Caesar" title="Julius Caesar">Julius Caesar</a> was <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Alexandria_(47_BC)" title="Siege of Alexandria (47 BC)">besieged at Alexandria</a>. His soldiers set fire to some of the Egyptian ships docked in the Alexandrian port while trying to clear the wharves to block the fleet belonging to <a href="/wiki/Cleopatra" title="Cleopatra">Cleopatra</a>'s brother <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy_XIV" class="mw-redirect" title="Ptolemy XIV">Ptolemy XIV</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>83<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-AulusGellius_86-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AulusGellius-86"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007_61-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This fire purportedly spread to the parts of the city nearest to the docks, causing considerable devastation in that area.<sup id="cite_ref-AulusGellius_86-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AulusGellius-86"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The first-century AD Roman playwright and Stoic philosopher <a href="/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger" title="Seneca the Younger">Seneca the Younger</a> quotes <a href="/wiki/Livy" title="Livy">Livy</a>'s <span title="Latin-language text"><i lang="la"><a href="/wiki/Ab_Urbe_Condita_Libri" class="mw-redirect" title="Ab Urbe Condita Libri">Ab Urbe Condita Libri</a></i></span>, which was written between 63 and 14 BC, as saying that the fire started by Caesar destroyed 40,000 scrolls from the Library of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007_61-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013150_87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013150-87"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>85<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Greek <a href="/wiki/Middle_Platonism" title="Middle Platonism">Middle Platonist</a> <a href="/wiki/Plutarch" title="Plutarch">Plutarch</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 46–120 AD) writes in his <i>Life of Caesar</i> that, "[W]hen the enemy endeavored to cut off his communication by sea, he was forced to divert that danger by setting fire to his ships, which, after burning the docks, thence spread on and destroyed the great library."<sup id="cite_ref-Plutarch_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Plutarch-88"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Roman historian <a href="/wiki/Cassius_Dio" title="Cassius Dio">Cassius Dio</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 155</span> – c.<span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 235 AD</span>), however, writes: "Many places were set on fire, with the result that, along with other buildings, the dockyards and storehouses of grain and books, said to be great in number and of the finest, were burned."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> However, <a href="/wiki/Florus" title="Florus">Florus</a> and <a href="/wiki/Lucan" title="Lucan">Lucan</a> only mention that the flames burned the fleet itself and some "houses near the sea".<sup id="cite_ref-El-AbbadiFathallah2008_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-El-AbbadiFathallah2008-90"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>88<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Scholars have interpreted Cassius Dio's wording to indicate that the fire did not actually destroy the entire Library itself, but rather one or more Library warehouses near the docks.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991256_91-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991256-91"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Whatever damage Caesar's fire may have caused, evidently the Library was not completely destroyed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991256_91-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991256-91"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The geographer <a href="/wiki/Strabo" title="Strabo">Strabo</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 63 BC</span> – c.<span style="white-space:nowrap;"> 24 AD</span>) mentions visiting the Mouseion, the larger research institution to which the Library was attached, in around 20 BC, several decades after Caesar's fire, indicating that it either survived the fire or was rebuilt soon afterwards.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Nonetheless, Strabo's manner of talking about the Mouseion shows that it was nowhere near as prestigious as it had been a few centuries prior. It is unknown whether this was due to historical decline or catastrophic destruction.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Despite mentioning the Mouseion, Strabo does not mention the Library separately, perhaps indicating that it had been so drastically reduced in stature and significance that Strabo felt it did not warrant separate mention.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011_8-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaughton2011-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It is unclear what happened to the Mouseion after Strabo's mention of it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007_61-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20007-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
