</p><p>Furthermore, Plutarch records in his <i>Life of Mark Antony</i> that in the years leading up to the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Actium" title="Battle of Actium">Battle of Actium</a> in 33 BC, <a href="/wiki/Mark_Antony" title="Mark Antony">Mark Antony</a> was rumored to have given Cleopatra all 200,000 scrolls in the Library of Pergamum.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Plutarch himself notes that his source for this anecdote was sometimes unreliable and it is possible that the story may be nothing more than propaganda intended to show that Mark Antony was loyal to Cleopatra and Egypt rather than to Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Casson, however, argues that even if the story was made up, it would not have been believable unless the Library still existed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Edward J. Watts argues that Mark Antony's gift may have been intended to replenish the Library's collection after the damage to it caused by Caesar's fire roughly a decade and a half prior.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Further evidence for the Library's survival after 48 BC comes from the fact that the most notable producer of composite commentaries during the late first century BC and early first century AD was a scholar who worked in Alexandria named <a href="/wiki/Didymus_Chalcenterus" title="Didymus Chalcenterus">Didymus Chalcenterus</a>, whose epithet <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><span lang="grc">Χαλκέντερος</span></span> (<span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><i lang="grc-Latn">Chalkénteros</i></span>) means "bronze guts".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20077_92-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20077-92"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Didymus is said to have produced somewhere between 3,500 and 4,000 books, making him the most prolific known writer in all of antiquity.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20077_92-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20077-92"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFox1986351_83-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFox1986351-83"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He was also given the nickname <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><span lang="grc">βιβλιολάθης</span></span> (<span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><i lang="grc-Latn">Biblioláthēs</i></span>), meaning "book-forgetter" because it was said that even he could not remember all the books he had written.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20077_92-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20077-92"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149–150_93-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKeown2013149–150-93"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Parts of some of Didymus' commentaries have been preserved in the forms of later extracts and these remains are modern scholars' most important sources of information about the critical works of the earlier scholars at the Library of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDickey20077_92-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDickey20077-92"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Lionel Casson states that Didymus' prodigious output "would have been impossible without at least a good part of the resources of the library at his disposal".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146_89-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Roman_period_and_destruction">Roman period and destruction</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Roman period and destruction"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Alexandria_Library_Inscription.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Alexandria_Library_Inscription.jpg/250px-Alexandria_Library_Inscription.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="291" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Alexandria_Library_Inscription.jpg/500px-Alexandria_Library_Inscription.jpg 2x" data-file-width="602" data-file-height="700"></a><figcaption>This Latin inscription regarding <a href="/wiki/Tiberius_Claudius_Balbilus" title="Tiberius Claudius Balbilus">Tiberius Claudius Balbilus</a> of Rome (d. c. AD 79) mentions the <span title="Latin-language text"><span lang="la" style="font-style: normal;">"ALEXANDRINA BYBLIOTHECE"</span></span> (line eight).</figcaption></figure>
<p>Very little is known about the Library of Alexandria during the time of the Roman <a href="/wiki/Principate" title="Principate">Principate</a> (27 BC – 284 AD).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The emperor <a href="/wiki/Claudius" title="Claudius">Claudius</a> (ruled 41–54 AD) is recorded to have built an extension to the Library,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200146–47_94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200146–47-94"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> but it seems that the Library of Alexandria's general fortunes followed those of the city of Alexandria itself.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009_95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After Alexandria came under Roman rule, the city's status and, consequently that of its famous Library, gradually diminished.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009_95-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> While the Mouseion still existed, membership was granted not on the basis of scholarly achievement, but rather on the basis of distinction in government, the military, or even in athletics.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The same was evidently the case even for the position of head librarian;<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> the only known head librarian from the Roman Period was a man named <a href="/wiki/Tiberius_Claudius_Balbilus" title="Tiberius Claudius Balbilus">Tiberius Claudius Balbilus</a>, who lived in the middle of the first century AD and was a politician, administrator, and military officer with no record of substantial scholarly achievements.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Members of the Mouseion were no longer required to teach, conduct research, or even live in Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008148_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008148-96"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Greek writer <a href="/wiki/Philostratus" title="Philostratus">Philostratus</a> records that the emperor <a href="/wiki/Hadrian" title="Hadrian">Hadrian</a> (ruled 117–138 AD) appointed the ethnographer Dionysius of Miletus and the sophist <a href="/wiki/Polemon_of_Laodicea" title="Polemon of Laodicea">Polemon of Laodicea</a> as members of the Mouseion, even though neither of these men is known to have ever spent any significant amount of time in Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008148_96-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008148-96"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>As the reputation of Alexandrian scholarship declined, the reputations of other libraries across the Mediterranean world improved, diminishing the Library of Alexandria's former status as the most prominent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009_95-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Other libraries also sprang up within the city of Alexandria itself<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and the scrolls from the Great Library may have been used to stock some of these smaller libraries.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Caesareum_of_Alexandria" title="Caesareum of Alexandria">Caesareum</a> and the Claudianum in Alexandria are both known to have had major libraries by the end of the first century AD.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149_82-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Serapeum, originally the "daughter library" of the Great Library, probably expanded during this period as well, according to classical historian Edward J. Watts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149–150_97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008149–150-97"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>By the second century AD, the Roman Empire grew less dependent on grain from Alexandria and the city's prominence declined further.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009_95-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Romans during this period also had less interest in Alexandrian scholarship, causing the Library's reputation to continue to decline as well.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009_95-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The scholars who worked and studied at the Library of Alexandria during the time of the Roman Empire were less well known than the ones who had studied there during the Ptolemaic Period.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009_95-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Eventually, the word "Alexandrian" itself came to be synonymous with the editing of texts, correction of textual errors, and writing of commentaries synthesized from those of earlier scholars—in other words, taking on connotations of pedantry, monotony, and lack of originality.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009_95-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20009-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Mention of both the Great Library of Alexandria and the Mouseion that housed it disappear after the middle of the third century AD.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The last known references to scholars being members of the Mouseion date to the 260s.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In 272 AD, the emperor <a href="/wiki/Aurelian" title="Aurelian">Aurelian</a> fought to recapture the city of Alexandria from the forces of the <a href="/wiki/Palmyrene_Empire" title="Palmyrene Empire">Palmyrene</a> queen <a href="/wiki/Zenobia" title="Zenobia">Zenobia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During the course of the fighting, Aurelian's forces destroyed the Broucheion quarter of the city in which the main library was located.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> If the Mouseion and Library still existed at this time, they were almost certainly destroyed or damaged during the attack.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200147_81-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200147-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> If they did survive the attack, whatever was left of them would have been further damaged or destroyed during the emperor <a href="/wiki/Diocletian" title="Diocletian">Diocletian</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Alexandria_(297%E2%80%93298)" title="Siege of Alexandria (297–298)">siege of Alexandria in 297</a>, when the Brouchion quarter was again destroyed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Arabic_sources_on_the_Arab_conquest">Arabic sources on the Arab conquest</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Arabic sources on the Arab conquest"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>In 642 AD, Alexandria was <a href="/wiki/Arab_conquest_of_Egypt" title="Arab conquest of Egypt">captured by an Arab army</a> under the command of <a href="/wiki/Amr_ibn_al-As" title="Amr ibn al-As">Amr ibn al-As</a>. Several later Arabic sources describe the library's destruction by the order of <a href="/wiki/Caliph_Omar" class="mw-redirect" title="Caliph Omar">Caliph Umar</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>97<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The earliest was <a href="/wiki/Al-Qifti" title="Al-Qifti">al-Qifti</a> who described the story in a biographical dictionary <i>History of Learned Men</i>, written before 1248.<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>98<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Bar-Hebraeus" class="mw-redirect" title="Bar-Hebraeus">Bar-Hebraeus</a>, writing in the thirteenth century, quotes Umar as saying to Yaḥyā al-Naḥwī (<a href="/wiki/John_Philoponus" title="John Philoponus">John Philoponus</a>): "If those books are in agreement with the <a href="/wiki/Quran" title="Quran">Quran</a>, we have no need of them; and if these are opposed to the Quran, destroy them." So, Ibn al Qifti recounts, the general ordered that the books be burned to fuel the fires that heated Alexandria's city baths. It is said that they were enough to provide heating for six months.<sup id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>99<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Later scholars, beginning with Father <a href="/wiki/Eus%C3%A8be_Renaudot" title="Eusèbe Renaudot">Eusèbe Renaudot</a> in his 1713 translation of the <i><a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Patriarchs_of_Alexandria" title="History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria">History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria</a></i>, are skeptical of these stories, given the amount of time that had passed before they were recorded and the political motivations of the various authors.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>101<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETrumbleMacIntyre_Marshall200351_104-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrumbleMacIntyre_Marshall200351-104"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Roy_MacLeod" title="Roy MacLeod">Roy MacLeod</a>, for example, points out that the story first appeared 500 years after the event, that John Philoponus was almost certainly dead by the time of the conquest of Egypt and that both the Great Library of Alexandria and the Mouseion were likely long gone by then.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod200071_105-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod200071-105"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>103<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to Diana Delia, "Omar's rejection of pagan and Christian wisdom may have been devised and exploited by conservative authorities as a moral exemplum for Muslims to follow in later, uncertain times, when the devotion of the faithful was once again tested by proximity to nonbelievers".<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The historian <a href="/wiki/Bernard_Lewis" title="Bernard Lewis">Bernard Lewis</a> suggests the myth came into existence during the reign of <a href="/wiki/Saladin" title="Saladin">Saladin</a> in order to justify the Sunni <a href="/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty" title="Ayyubid dynasty">Ayyubids</a>' breaking up of the Shia <a href="/wiki/Fatimid_Caliphate" title="Fatimid Caliphate">Fatimid</a> collections and library at public auction.<sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Successors_to_the_Mouseion">Successors to the Mouseion</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Successors to the Mouseion"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Alexandrian_World_Chronicle_-_6v.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Alexandrian_World_Chronicle_-_6v.jpg/250px-Alexandrian_World_Chronicle_-_6v.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="273" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Alexandrian_World_Chronicle_-_6v.jpg/500px-Alexandrian_World_Chronicle_-_6v.jpg 2x" data-file-width="843" data-file-height="920"></a><figcaption>Drawing from the <a href="/wiki/Alexandrian_World_Chronicle" title="Alexandrian World Chronicle">Alexandrian World Chronicle</a> depicting Pope <a href="/wiki/Theophilus_I_of_Alexandria" title="Theophilus I of Alexandria">Theophilus I of Alexandria</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gospel" title="Gospel">gospel</a> in hand, standing triumphantly atop the <a href="/wiki/Serapeum_of_Alexandria" title="Serapeum of Alexandria">Serapeum</a> in 391 AD<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts201760_108-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts201760-108"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>106<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Serapeum">Serapeum</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Serapeum"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The Serapeum is often called the "Daughter Library"<sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> of Alexandria. For much of the late fourth century AD it was probably the largest collection of books in the city of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150,_189_110-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150,_189-110"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>108<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In the 370s and 380s, the Serapeum was still a major pilgrimage site for pagans.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189_111-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189-111"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It remained a fully functioning temple, and had classrooms for philosophers to teach in.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189_111-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189-111"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It naturally tended to attract followers of <a href="/wiki/Iamblichus" title="Iamblichus">Iamblichean</a> <a href="/wiki/Neoplatonism" title="Neoplatonism">Neoplatonism</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189_111-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189-111"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Most of these philosophers were primarily interested in <a href="/wiki/Theurgy" title="Theurgy">theurgy</a>, the study of cultic rituals and esoteric religious practices.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189_111-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189-111"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Neoplatonist philosopher <a href="/wiki/Damascius" title="Damascius">Damascius</a> (lived <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 458 – after 538) records that a man named Olympus came from <a href="/wiki/Cilicia" title="Cilicia">Cilicia</a> to teach at the Serapeum, where he enthusiastically taught his students the rules of traditional divine worship and ancient religious practices.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189–190_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008189–190-112"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>110<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He enjoined his students to worship the old gods in traditional ways, and he may have even taught them theurgy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190_113-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Scattered references indicate that, sometime in the fourth century, an institution known as the "Mouseion" may have been reestablished at a different location somewhere in Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Nothing, however, is known about the characteristics of this organization.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It may have possessed some bibliographic resources, but whatever they may have been, they were clearly not comparable to those of its predecessor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150–151_114-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150–151-114"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>112<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Under the Christian rule of Roman emperor <a href="/wiki/Theodosius_I" title="Theodosius I">Theodosius I</a>, pagan rituals were outlawed, and pagan temples were destroyed. In 391 AD, the bishop of Alexandria, Theophilus, supervised the destruction of an old <a href="/wiki/Mithraeum" title="Mithraeum">Mithraeum</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190_113-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> They gave some of the cult objects to <a href="/wiki/Pope_Theophilus_I_of_Alexandria" class="mw-redirect" title="Pope Theophilus I of Alexandria">Theophilus</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190_113-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> who had them paraded through the streets so that they could be mocked and ridiculed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190_113-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The pagans of Alexandria were incensed by this act of desecration, especially the teachers of Neoplatonic philosophy and theurgy at the Serapeum.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190_113-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The teachers at the Serapeum took up arms and led their students and other followers in a <a href="/wiki/Guerrilla_warfare" title="Guerrilla warfare">guerrilla attack</a> on the Christian population of Alexandria, killing many of them before being forced to retreat.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190_113-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008190-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In retaliation, the Christians vandalized and demolished the Serapeum,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191_115-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191-115"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETheodore2016182–183_116-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETheodore2016182–183-116"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> although some parts of the <a href="/wiki/Colonnade" title="Colonnade">colonnade</a> were still standing as late as the twelfth century.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191_115-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191-115"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Whether an actual library still existed at this point, and if so how extensive it was, is not recorded. Jonathan Theodore has stated that by 391/392 AD there was "no remaining "Great Library" in the sense of the iconic vast, priceless collection".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETheodore2016182–183_116-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETheodore2016182–183-116"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Only Orosius explicitly mentions the destruction of books or scrolls; sources probably written after the Serapeum's destruction speak of its collection of literature in the past tense.<sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>115<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-118"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>116<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On the other hand, a recent article identifies the literary evidence suggesting that the original Ptolemaic library collection was moved to the Serapeum by the end of the second century AD and that a library is attested there until the Serapeum was destroyed along with the books it contained.<sup id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-119"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="School_of_Theon_and_Hypatia">School of Theon and Hypatia</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: School of Theon and Hypatia"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Hypatia_(Charles_Mitchell).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Hypatia_%28Charles_Mitchell%29.jpg/250px-Hypatia_%28Charles_Mitchell%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="402" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.75" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Hypatia_%28Charles_Mitchell%29.jpg/500px-Hypatia_%28Charles_Mitchell%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1982" data-file-height="3186"></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Hypatia_(painting)" title="Hypatia (painting)">Hypatia</a></i> (1885) by <a href="/wiki/Charles_William_Mitchell" title="Charles William Mitchell">Charles William Mitchell</a>, believed to be a depiction of a scene in <a href="/wiki/Charles_Kingsley" title="Charles Kingsley">Charles Kingsley</a>'s 1853 novel <i><a href="/wiki/Hypatia_(novel)" title="Hypatia (novel)">Hypatia</a></i><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBooth201721–22_120-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBooth201721–22-120"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>118<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>The <i><a href="/wiki/Suda" title="Suda">Suda</a></i>, a tenth-century <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine</a> encyclopedia, calls the mathematician <a href="/wiki/Theon_of_Alexandria" title="Theon of Alexandria">Theon of Alexandria</a> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> AD 335–<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 405) a "man of the Mouseion".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191–192_121-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191–192-121"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to classical historian Edward J. Watts, however, Theon was probably the head of a school called the "Mouseion", which was named in emulation of the <a href="/wiki/Hellenistic_period" title="Hellenistic period">Hellenistic</a> Mouseion that had once included the Library of Alexandria, but which had little other connection to it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191–192_121-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191–192-121"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Theon's school was exclusive, highly prestigious, and doctrinally conservative.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008192_122-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008192-122"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Theon does not seem to have had any connections to the militant Iamblichean Neoplatonists who taught in the Serapeum.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191_115-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008191-115"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Instead, he seems to have rejected the teachings of Iamblichus<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008192_122-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008192-122"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and may have taken pride in teaching a pure, <a href="/wiki/Plotinus" title="Plotinus">Plotinian</a> Neoplatonism.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008192_122-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008192-122"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In around 400 AD, Theon's daughter <a href="/wiki/Hypatia" title="Hypatia">Hypatia</a> (born c. 350–370; died 415 AD) succeeded him as the head of his school.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEOakes2007364_123-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOakes2007364-123"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>121<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Like her father, she rejected the teachings of Iamblichus and instead embraced the original Neoplatonism formulated by Plotinus.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008192_122-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008192-122"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Theophilus, the bishop involved in the destruction of the Serapeum, tolerated Hypatia's school and even encouraged two of her students to become bishops in territory under his authority.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008196_124-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008196-124"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>122<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Hypatia was extremely popular with the people of Alexandria<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008195–196_125-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008195–196-125"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>123<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and exerted profound political influence.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008195–196_125-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008195–196-125"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>123<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Theophilus respected Alexandria's political structures and raised no objection to the close ties Hypatia established with Roman prefects.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008196_124-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008196-124"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>122<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Hypatia was later implicated in a political feud between <a href="/wiki/Orestes_(prefect)" class="mw-redirect" title="Orestes (prefect)">Orestes</a>, the <a href="/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Roman_Egypt" title="List of governors of Roman Egypt">Roman prefect of Alexandria</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Cyril_of_Alexandria" title="Cyril of Alexandria">Cyril of Alexandria</a>, Theophilus' successor as bishop.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENovak2010240_126-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENovak2010240-126"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>124<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECameronLongSherry199358–61_127-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameronLongSherry199358–61-127"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>125<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rumors spread accusing her of preventing Orestes from reconciling with Cyril<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENovak2010240_126-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENovak2010240-126"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>124<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECameronLongSherry199359_128-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameronLongSherry199359-128"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>126<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and, in March of 415 AD, she was murdered by a mob of Christians, led by a <a href="/wiki/Reader_(liturgy)" title="Reader (liturgy)">lector</a> named Peter.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENovak2010240_126-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENovak2010240-126"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>124<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECameronLongSherry199359–61_129-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECameronLongSherry199359–61-129"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>127<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> She had no successor and her school collapsed after her death.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2017117_130-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2017117-130"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>128<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Later_schools_and_libraries_in_Alexandria">Later schools and libraries in Alexandria</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: Later schools and libraries in Alexandria"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Nonetheless, Hypatia was not the last pagan in Alexandria, nor was she the last Neoplatonist philosopher.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBooth2017151–152_131-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBooth2017151–152-131"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>129<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2017154–155_132-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2017154–155-132"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>130<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Neoplatonism and paganism both survived in Alexandria and throughout the eastern Mediterranean for centuries after her death.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBooth2017151–152_131-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBooth2017151–152-131"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>129<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2017154–155_132-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2017154–155-132"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>130<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> British Egyptologist <a href="/wiki/Charlotte_Booth" title="Charlotte Booth">Charlotte Booth</a> notes that many new academic lecture halls were built in Alexandria at Kom el-Dikka shortly after Hypatia's death, indicating that philosophy was clearly still taught in Alexandrian schools.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBooth2017151_133-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBooth2017151-133"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>131<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The late fifth-century writers <a href="/wiki/Zacharias_Scholasticus" class="mw-redirect" title="Zacharias Scholasticus">Zacharias Scholasticus</a> and <a href="/wiki/Aeneas_of_Gaza" title="Aeneas of Gaza">Aeneas of Gaza</a> both speak of the "Mouseion" as occupying some kind of a physical space.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Archaeologists have identified lecture halls dating to around this time period, located near, but not on, the site of the Ptolemaic Mouseion, which may be the "Mouseion" to which these writers refer.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150_98-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatts2008150-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Collection">Collection</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: Collection"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>It is not possible to determine the collection's size in any era with certainty. <a href="/wiki/Papyrus" title="Papyrus">Papyrus</a> scrolls constituted the collection, and although <a href="/wiki/Codex" title="Codex">codices</a> were used after 300 BC, the Alexandrian Library is never documented as having switched to <a href="/wiki/Parchment" title="Parchment">parchment</a>, perhaps because of its strong links to the papyrus trade. The Library of Alexandria in fact was indirectly causal in the creation of writing on parchment, as the Egyptians refused to export papyrus to their competitor in the <a href="/wiki/Library_of_Pergamum" title="Library of Pergamum">Library of Pergamum</a>. Consequently, the Library of Pergamum developed parchment as its own writing material.<sup id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-134"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>132<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>A single piece of writing might occupy several scrolls, and this division into self-contained "books" was a major aspect of editorial work. King <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy_II_Philadelphus" title="Ptolemy II Philadelphus">Ptolemy II Philadelphus</a> (309–246 BC) is said to have set 500,000 scrolls as an objective for the library.<sup id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-135"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>133<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The library's index, <a href="/wiki/Callimachus" title="Callimachus">Callimachus</a>' <i><a href="/wiki/Pinakes" title="Pinakes">Pinakes</a></i>, has only survived in the form of a few fragments, and it is not possible to know with certainty how large and how diverse the collection may have been. At its height, the library was said to possess nearly half a million scrolls, and, although historians debate the precise number, the highest estimates claim 900,000 scrolls<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> while the most conservative estimates are as low as 40,000,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWiegandDavis201520_6-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWiegandDavis201520-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010_3-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillips2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> which is still an enormous collection that required vast storage space.<sup id="cite_ref-Murray_136-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Murray-136"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>134<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>As a research institution, the library filled its stacks with new works in mathematics, astronomy, physics, natural sciences, and other subjects. Its empirical standards were applied in one of the first and certainly strongest homes for serious <a href="/wiki/Textual_criticism" title="Textual criticism">textual criticism</a>. As the same text often existed in several different versions, comparative textual criticism was crucial for ensuring their veracity. Once ascertained, canonical copies would then be made for scholars, royalty, and wealthy bibliophiles all over the world, this commerce bringing income to the library.<sup id="cite_ref-Kennedy1999_41-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Kennedy1999-41"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Legacy">Legacy</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Legacy"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="In_antiquity">In antiquity</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=19" title="Edit section: In antiquity"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The Library of Alexandria was one of the largest and most prestigious libraries of the ancient world, but it was far from the only one.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGarland200860_7-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarland200860-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20003,_10–11_137-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20003,_10–11-137"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>135<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECasson200148_138-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson200148-138"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>136<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> By the end of the Hellenistic Period, almost every city in the Eastern Mediterranean had a public library and so did many medium-sized towns.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGarland200860_7-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarland200860-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20003_4-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod20003-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During the Roman Period, the number of libraries only proliferated.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533_139-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> By the fourth century AD, there were at least two dozen public libraries in the city of Rome alone.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533_139-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As the Library of Alexandria declined, centers of academic excellence arose in various other capital cities. It is possible most of the material from the Library of Alexandria survived, by way of the <a href="/wiki/Imperial_Library_of_Constantinople" title="Imperial Library of Constantinople">Imperial Library of Constantinople</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Academy_of_Gondishapur" title="Academy of Gondishapur">Academy of Gondishapur</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Wisdom" title="House of Wisdom">House of Wisdom</a>. This material may then have been preserved by the <a href="/wiki/Reconquista" title="Reconquista">Reconquista</a>, which led to the formation of <a href="/wiki/Medieval_university" title="Medieval university">European universities</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Research_library#Renaissance" title="Research library">recompilation of ancient texts</a> from formerly scattered fragments.<sup id="cite_ref-140" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-140"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>138<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In late antiquity, as the Roman Empire became Christianized, Christian libraries modeled directly on the Library of Alexandria and other great libraries of earlier pagan times began to be founded all across the Greek-speaking eastern part of the empire.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533_139-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Among the largest and most prominent of these libraries were the <a href="/wiki/Theological_Library_of_Caesarea_Maritima" title="Theological Library of Caesarea Maritima">Theological Library of Caesarea Maritima</a>, the Library of Jerusalem, and a Christian library in Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533_139-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> These libraries held both pagan and Christian writings side-by-side<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533_139-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and Christian scholars applied to the Christian scriptures the same philological techniques that the scholars of the Library of Alexandria had used for analyzing the Greek classics.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533_139-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Nonetheless, the study of pagan authors remained secondary to the study of the Christian scriptures until the <a href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533_139-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Maqamat_hariri.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Maqamat_hariri.jpg/250px-Maqamat_hariri.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="254" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Maqamat_hariri.jpg/500px-Maqamat_hariri.jpg 2x" data-file-width="974" data-file-height="989"></a><figcaption>Illustration by <a href="/wiki/Yahya_ibn_Mahmud_al-Wasiti" title="Yahya ibn Mahmud al-Wasiti">Yahyá al-Wasiti</a> from 1237 depicting scholars at an <a href="/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate" title="Abbasid Caliphate">Abbasid</a> library in <a href="/wiki/Baghdad" title="Baghdad">Baghdad</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The survival of ancient texts owes a great deal to the fact that they were exhaustingly copied and recopied. At first, they were copied by professional scribes during the Roman period.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGarland200861_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarland200861-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533–534_141-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533–534-141"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>139<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Mediaeval Muslim scholars also played a crucial role in preserving and translating the knowledge of the ancient world.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWebster1933466_142-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebster1933466-142"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>140<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Graeco-Arabic_translation_movement" title="Graeco-Arabic translation movement">Graeco-Arabic translation movement</a> translated a significant number of ancient texts into Arabic, keeping the texts intact and preserving them.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAhmedAhsani200574-77_143-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAhmedAhsani200574-77-143"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>141<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Later, they were translated and re-introduced to Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAhmedAhsani200574-77_143-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAhmedAhsani200574-77-143"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>141<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This movement began in earnest under the <a href="/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphs" class="mw-redirect" title="Abbasid Caliphs">Abbasid Caliphate</a> where it played a significant role in the <a href="/wiki/Islamic_Golden_Age" title="Islamic Golden Age">Islamic Golden Age</a>. The translation movement encompassed scholars of various religions in the Abbasid empire. For example, under the patronage of Caliph <a href="/wiki/Al-Ma%27mun" title="Al-Ma'mun">al-Ma'mun</a>, a Christian scholar and translator named <a href="/wiki/Hunayn_ibn_Ishaq" title="Hunayn ibn Ishaq">Hunayn ibn Ishaq</a> completed major translation projects of Aristotle, Hypocrates, and Galen<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAhmedAhsani200574-77_143-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAhmedAhsani200574-77-143"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>141<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>  so that they remained accessible to scholars. These translations were translated into Latin and re-introduced to Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAhmedAhsani200574-77_143-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAhmedAhsani200574-77-143"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>141<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> These texts were copied by monks during <a href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</a> and <a href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</a>, making them more easily available to European scholars once more.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGarland200861_1-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarland200861-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENelles2010533–534_141-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelles2010533–534-141"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>139<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Modern_library:_Bibliotheca_Alexandrina">Modern library: Bibliotheca Alexandrina</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Library_of_Alexandria&action=edit&section=20" title="Edit section: Modern library: Bibliotheca Alexandrina"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1320445320"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Bibliotheca_Alexandrina" title="Bibliotheca Alexandrina">Bibliotheca Alexandrina</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:CW_BibliotechaAlexandrina_Inside.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/CW_BibliotechaAlexandrina_Inside.jpg/250px-CW_BibliotechaAlexandrina_Inside.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/CW_BibliotechaAlexandrina_Inside.jpg/500px-CW_BibliotechaAlexandrina_Inside.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1000" data-file-height="667"></a><figcaption>Interior of the modern <a href="/wiki/Bibliotheca_Alexandrina" title="Bibliotheca Alexandrina">Bibliotheca Alexandrina</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The idea of reviving the ancient Library of Alexandria in the modern era was first proposed in 1974, after Lotfy Dowidar was president of the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Alexandria" class="mw-redirect" title="University of Alexandria">University of Alexandria</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265_144-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265-144"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>142<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In May 1986, Egypt requested the executive board of <a href="/wiki/UNESCO" title="UNESCO">UNESCO</a> to allow the international organization to conduct a feasibility study for the project.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265_144-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265-144"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>142<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This marked the beginning of UNESCO and the international community's involvement in trying to bring the project to fruition.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265_144-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265-144"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>142<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Starting in 1988, UNESCO and the <a href="/wiki/UNDP" class="mw-redirect" title="UNDP">UNDP</a> worked to support the international architectural competition to design the Library.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265_144-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265-144"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>142<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Egypt devoted four hectares of land for the building of the Library and established the National High Commission for the Library of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265–266_145-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991265–266-145"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>143<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Egyptian president <a href="/wiki/Hosni_Mubarak" title="Hosni Mubarak">Hosni Mubarak</a> took a personal interest in the project, which greatly contributed to its advancement.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991266_146-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991266-146"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>144<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An international architectural competition took place in 1989 with Norwegian architectural firm <a href="/wiki/Sn%C3%B8hetta_(company)" title="Snøhetta (company)">Snøhetta</a> winning the competition.<sup id="cite_ref-147" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-147"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>145<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Completed in 2002, the <a href="/wiki/Bibliotheca_Alexandrina" title="Bibliotheca Alexandrina">Bibliotheca Alexandrina</a> now functions as a modern library and cultural center, commemorating the original Library of Alexandria.<sup id="cite_ref-148" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-148"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>146<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In line with the mission of the Great Library of Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina also houses the <a href="/wiki/International_School_of_Information_Science" title="International School of Information Science">International School of Information Science</a>, a school for students preparing for highly specialized post-graduate degrees, whose goal is to train professional staff for libraries in Egypt and across the Middle East.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991259_149-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETocatlian1991259-149"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>147<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
