Salvatore ad Sancta Sanctorum, who then inhabited a northern portion of it until as late as the early 19th century.<sup id="cite_ref-History_of_the_Colosseum_25-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-History_of_the_Colosseum-25"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-colnet_26-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-colnet-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The interior of the amphitheater was extensively stripped of stone, which was reused elsewhere, or (in the case of the marble façade) was burned to make <a href="/wiki/Quicklime" class="mw-redirect" title="Quicklime">quicklime</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The iron clamps<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> which held the stonework together were pried or hacked out of the walls, leaving numerous pockmarks which still scar the building today.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Modern">Modern</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Maarten_van_Heemskerck_-_Rome,_the_Colosseum.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Maarten_van_Heemskerck_-_Rome%2C_the_Colosseum.jpg/250px-Maarten_van_Heemskerck_-_Rome%2C_the_Colosseum.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="161" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Maarten_van_Heemskerck_-_Rome%2C_the_Colosseum.jpg/500px-Maarten_van_Heemskerck_-_Rome%2C_the_Colosseum.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2500" data-file-height="1613"></a><figcaption>The Colosseum in the 1530s, sketched by <a href="/wiki/Maarten_van_Heemskerck" title="Maarten van Heemskerck">Maarten van Heemskerck</a>, and used as the model for his later <i><a href="/wiki/Self-Portrait_with_the_Colosseum" title="Self-Portrait with the Colosseum">Self-Portrait with the Colosseum</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Octo_Mundi_Miracula" title="Octo Mundi Miracula">Octo Mundi Miracula</a></i>.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Piranesi_Kolosseum.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Piranesi_Kolosseum.jpg/330px-Piranesi_Kolosseum.jpg" decoding="async" width="330" height="230" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.2" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Piranesi_Kolosseum.jpg/960px-Piranesi_Kolosseum.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4676" data-file-height="3261"></a><figcaption>Overview of the interior of the Colosseum in a 1776 engraving by <a href="/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Piranesi" title="Giovanni Battista Piranesi">Giovanni Battista Piranesi</a></figcaption></figure> 
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Colosseum_and_Arch_of_Constantine_(est._1870).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Colosseum_and_Arch_of_Constantine_%28est._1870%29.jpg/250px-Colosseum_and_Arch_of_Constantine_%28est._1870%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="183" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Colosseum_and_Arch_of_Constantine_%28est._1870%29.jpg/500px-Colosseum_and_Arch_of_Constantine_%28est._1870%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1900" data-file-height="1389"></a><figcaption>1870 view emphasizing the semi-rural environs of the Colosseum at the time</figcaption></figure>
<p>During the 16th and 17th century, Church officials sought a productive role for the Colosseum. <a href="/wiki/Pope_Sixtus_V" title="Pope Sixtus V">Pope Sixtus V</a> (1585–1590) planned to turn the building into a wool factory to provide employment for Rome's prostitutes, though this proposal fell through with his premature death.<sup id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 1671, Cardinal <a href="/wiki/Paluzzo_Paluzzi_Altieri_degli_Albertoni" title="Paluzzo Paluzzi Altieri degli Albertoni">Paluzzo Altieri</a> authorized its use for <a href="/wiki/Bullfight" class="mw-redirect" title="Bullfight">bullfights</a>; a public outcry caused the idea to be hastily abandoned.<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>28<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:The_British_Army_on_Leave_in_Italy,_June_1944_TR1959.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/The_British_Army_on_Leave_in_Italy%2C_June_1944_TR1959.jpg/250px-The_British_Army_on_Leave_in_Italy%2C_June_1944_TR1959.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="379" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.75" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/The_British_Army_on_Leave_in_Italy%2C_June_1944_TR1959.jpg/500px-The_British_Army_on_Leave_in_Italy%2C_June_1944_TR1959.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1637" data-file-height="2480"></a><figcaption>Allied troops consult a guidebook outside the Colosseum after liberation in 1944</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1749, <a href="/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XIV" title="Pope Benedict XIV">Pope Benedict XIV</a> endorsed the view that the Colosseum was a sacred site where early Christians had been <a href="/wiki/Martyr" title="Martyr">martyred</a>. He forbade the use of the Colosseum as a quarry and consecrated the building to the <a href="/wiki/Passion_(Christianity)" class="mw-redirect" title="Passion (Christianity)">Passion of Christ</a> and installed <a href="/wiki/Stations_of_the_Cross" title="Stations of the Cross">Stations of the Cross</a>, declaring it sanctified by the blood of the <a href="/wiki/Persecution_of_early_Christians_by_the_Romans" class="mw-redirect" title="Persecution of early Christians by the Romans">Christian martyrs</a> who perished there (<i>see <a href="#Significance_in_Christianity">Significance in Christianity</a></i>).
</p><p>However, there is no historical evidence to support Benedict's claim, nor is there even any evidence that anyone before the 16th century suggested this might be the case; the <i><a href="/wiki/Catholic_Encyclopedia" title="Catholic Encyclopedia">Catholic Encyclopedia</a></i> concludes that there are no historical grounds for the supposition, other than the reasonably plausible conjecture that some of the many martyrs may well have been Christian.<sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Cole_Thomas_Interior_of_the_Colosseum_Rome_1832.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Cole_Thomas_Interior_of_the_Colosseum_Rome_1832.jpg/250px-Cole_Thomas_Interior_of_the_Colosseum_Rome_1832.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="137" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Cole_Thomas_Interior_of_the_Colosseum_Rome_1832.jpg/500px-Cole_Thomas_Interior_of_the_Colosseum_Rome_1832.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1000" data-file-height="549"></a><figcaption><i>Interior of the Colosseum, Rome</i> (1832) by <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Cole" title="Thomas Cole">Thomas Cole</a>, showing the <a href="/wiki/Stations_of_the_Cross" title="Stations of the Cross">Stations of the Cross</a> around the arena and the extensive vegetation</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Colosseum,_Eastern_Interior.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Colosseum%2C_Eastern_Interior.jpg/250px-Colosseum%2C_Eastern_Interior.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Colosseum%2C_Eastern_Interior.jpg/500px-Colosseum%2C_Eastern_Interior.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5872" data-file-height="3915"></a><figcaption>Eastern interior (viewed from west), 2023</figcaption></figure>
<p>Later popes initiated various stabilization and restoration projects, removing the extensive vegetation which had overgrown the structure and threatened to damage it further. The façade was reinforced with triangular brick wedges in 1807 and 1827, and the interior was repaired in 1831, 1846 and in the 1930s. The arena substructure was partly excavated in 1810–1814 and 1874 and was fully exposed under <a href="/wiki/Benito_Mussolini" title="Benito Mussolini">Benito Mussolini</a> in the 1930s.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The Colosseum is today one of Rome's most popular tourist attractions, receiving millions of visitors annually.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (December 2024)">citation needed</span></a></i>]</sup> The effects of pollution and general deterioration over time prompted a major restoration programme carried out between 1993 and 2000, at a cost of 40 billion <a href="/wiki/Italian_lira" title="Italian lira">lire</a> ($19.3 million or €20.6 million at 2000 prices).<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (December 2024)">citation needed</span></a></i>]</sup>
</p><p>In recent years, the Colosseum has become a symbol of the international campaign against capital punishment, which was abolished in Italy in 1948. Several anti–death penalty demonstrations took place in front of the Colosseum in 2000. Since that time, as a gesture against the death penalty, the local authorities of Rome change the color of the Colosseum's night time illumination from white to gold whenever a person condemned to the death penalty anywhere in the world gets their sentence commuted or is released,<sup id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> or if a jurisdiction abolishes the death penalty. Most recently, the Colosseum was illuminated in gold in November 2012 following the abolishment of capital punishment in the American state of <a href="/wiki/Connecticut" title="Connecticut">Connecticut</a> in April 2012.<sup id="cite_ref-Death_Penalty_31-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Death_Penalty-31"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Because of the ruined state of the interior, it is impractical to use the Colosseum to host large events; only a few hundred spectators can be accommodated in temporary seating. However, much larger concerts have been held just outside, using the Colosseum as a backdrop. Performers who have played at the Colosseum in recent years have included <a href="/wiki/Ray_Charles" title="Ray Charles">Ray Charles</a> (May 2002),<sup id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Paul_McCartney" title="Paul McCartney">Paul McCartney</a> (May 2003),<sup id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Elton_John" title="Elton John">Elton John</a> (September 2005),<sup id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Billy_Joel" title="Billy Joel">Billy Joel</a> (July 2006).
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Physical_description">Physical description</h2></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Exterior">Exterior</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Colosseum_exterior,_inner_and_outer_wall_AvL.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Colosseum_exterior%2C_inner_and_outer_wall_AvL.jpg/250px-Colosseum_exterior%2C_inner_and_outer_wall_AvL.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="119" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Colosseum_exterior%2C_inner_and_outer_wall_AvL.jpg/500px-Colosseum_exterior%2C_inner_and_outer_wall_AvL.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3648" data-file-height="1740"></a><figcaption>The exterior of the Colosseum, showing the partially intact outer wall (left) and the mostly intact inner wall (center and right)</figcaption></figure>
<p>Unlike <a href="/wiki/Roman_theatre_(structure)" title="Roman theatre (structure)">Roman theatres</a> that were built into hillsides, the Colosseum is an entirely free-standing structure. It derives its basic exterior and interior architecture from that of two theatres back to back. It is elliptical in plan and is 189 meters (615 ft / 640 Roman feet) long, and 156 meters (510 ft / 528 Roman feet) wide, with a base area of 24,000 square metres (6 acres). The height of the outer wall is 48 meters (157 ft / 165 Roman feet). The perimeter originally measured 545 meters (1,788 ft / 1,835 Roman feet). The central arena is an ellipse 87 m (287 ft) long and 55 m (180 ft) wide, surrounded by a wall 5 m (15 ft) high, above which rose tiers of seating.
</p><p>The outer wall is estimated to have required over 100,000 cubic metres (3.5 million <a href="/wiki/Cubic_foot" title="Cubic foot">cubic feet</a>) of <a href="/wiki/Travertine" title="Travertine">travertine</a> stone which were set without mortar; they were held together by 300 tons of iron clamps.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> However, it has suffered extensive damage over the centuries, with large segments having collapsed following earthquakes. The north side of the perimeter wall is still standing; the distinctive triangular brick wedges at each end are modern additions, having been constructed in the early 19th century to shore up the wall. The remainder of the present-day exterior of the Colosseum is in fact the original interior wall.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Exterior_of_the_Colosseum_01.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Exterior_of_the_Colosseum_01.JPG/250px-Exterior_of_the_Colosseum_01.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Exterior_of_the_Colosseum_01.JPG/500px-Exterior_of_the_Colosseum_01.JPG 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="3000"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Superposed_order" title="Superposed order">Superposed order</a> of the Colosseum</figcaption></figure>
<p>The surviving part of the outer wall's monumental façade comprises three <a href="/wiki/Superposed_order" title="Superposed order">superposed</a> storeys surmounted by a <a href="/wiki/Podium" title="Podium">podium</a> on which stands a tall <a href="/wiki/Attic" title="Attic">attic</a>, both of which are pierced by windows interspersed at regular intervals. The arcades are framed by half-columns of the <a href="/wiki/Doric_order" title="Doric order">Doric</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ionic_order" title="Ionic order">Ionic</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Corinthian_order" title="Corinthian order">Corinthian</a> orders, while the attic is decorated with Corinthian <a href="/wiki/Pilaster" title="Pilaster">pilasters</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-oxford_classical_35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-oxford_classical-35"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Each of the arches in the second- and third-floor arcades framed statues, probably honoring divinities and other figures from <a href="/wiki/Classical_mythology" title="Classical mythology">Classical mythology</a>.
</p><p>Two hundred and forty mast <a href="/wiki/Corbel" title="Corbel">corbels</a> were positioned around the top of the attic. They originally supported a retractable <a href="/wiki/Awning" title="Awning">awning</a>, known as the <i><a href="/wiki/Velarium" title="Velarium">velarium</a></i>, that kept the sun and rain off spectators. This consisted of a canvas-covered, net-like structure made of ropes, with a hole in the center.<sup id="cite_ref-roth_3-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-roth-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It covered two-thirds of the arena, and sloped down towards the center to catch the wind and provide a breeze for the audience. Sailors, specially enlisted from the Roman naval headquarters at <a href="/wiki/Misenum" class="mw-redirect" title="Misenum">Misenum</a> and housed in the nearby <i>Castra Misenatium</i>, were used to work the <i><a href="/wiki/Velarium" title="Velarium">velarium</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Colosseum-Entrance_LII.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Colosseum-Entrance_LII.jpg/250px-Colosseum-Entrance_LII.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Colosseum-Entrance_LII.jpg/500px-Colosseum-Entrance_LII.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="768"></a><figcaption>Entrance LII of the Colosseum, with <a href="/wiki/Roman_numerals" title="Roman numerals">Roman numerals</a> still visible</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Colosseum's huge crowd capacity made it essential that the venue could be filled or evacuated quickly. Its architects adopted solutions very similar to those used in modern stadia to deal with the same problem. The amphitheatre was ringed by eighty entrances at ground level, 76 of which were used by ordinary spectators.<sup id="cite_ref-roth_3-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-roth-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Each entrance and exit was numbered, as was each staircase. The northern main entrance was reserved for the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Emperor" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Emperor">Roman Emperor</a> and his aides, whilst the other three axial entrances were most likely used by the elite. All four axial entrances were richly decorated with painted <a href="/wiki/Stucco" title="Stucco">stucco</a> reliefs, of which fragments survive. Many of the original outer entrances have disappeared with the collapse of the perimeter wall, but entrances XXIII (23) to LIIII (54) survive.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Spectators were given tickets in the form of numbered pottery shards, which directed them to the appropriate section and row. They accessed their seats via <i><a href="/wiki/Vomitorium" title="Vomitorium">vomitoria</a></i> (singular <i>vomitorium</i>), passageways that opened into a tier of seats from below or behind. These quickly dispersed people into their seats and, upon conclusion of the event or in an emergency evacuation, could permit their exit within only a few minutes. The name <i>vomitoria</i> derived from the Latin word for a rapid discharge, from which English derives the word vomit.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Interior_seating">Interior seating</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Rome_(29096723).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Rome_%2829096723%29.jpg/250px-Rome_%2829096723%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Rome_%2829096723%29.jpg/500px-Rome_%2829096723%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1944"></a><figcaption>The raked areas that once held seating</figcaption></figure>
<p>According to the <a href="/wiki/Chronography_of_354" class="mw-redirect" title="Chronography of 354">Codex-Calendar of 354</a>, the Colosseum could accommodate 87,000 people, although modern estimates put the figure at around 50,000. They were seated in a tiered arrangement that reflected the rigidly stratified nature of Roman society. Special boxes were provided at the north and south ends respectively for the Emperor and the <a href="/wiki/Vestal_Virgins" class="mw-redirect" title="Vestal Virgins">Vestal Virgins</a>, providing the best views of the arena. Flanking them at the same level was a broad platform or <i>podium</i> for the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Senate" title="Roman Senate">senatorial</a> class, who were allowed to bring their own chairs. The names of some 5th century senators can still be seen carved into the stonework, presumably reserving areas for their use.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Colosseum-profile-english.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Colosseum-profile-english.png/250px-Colosseum-profile-english.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="194" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Colosseum-profile-english.png/500px-Colosseum-profile-english.png 2x" data-file-width="1550" data-file-height="1200"></a><figcaption>Diagram of the levels of seating</figcaption></figure>
<p>The tier above the senators, known as the <i>maenianum primum</i>, was occupied by the non-senatorial noble class or knights (<i><a href="/wiki/Equestrian_(Roman)" class="mw-redirect" title="Equestrian (Roman)">equites</a></i>). The next level up, the <i>maenianum secundum</i>, was originally reserved for ordinary Roman citizens (<i><a href="/wiki/Plebs" class="mw-redirect" title="Plebs">plebeians</a></i>) and was divided into two sections. The lower part (the <i>immum</i>) was for wealthy citizens, while the upper part (the <i>summum</i>) was for poor citizens. Specific sectors were provided for other social groups: for instance, boys with their tutors, soldiers on leave, foreign dignitaries, scribes, heralds, priests and so on. Stone (and later marble) seating was provided for the citizens and nobles, who presumably would have brought their own cushions with them. Inscriptions identified the areas reserved for specific groups.
</p><p>Another level, the <i>maenianum secundum in legneis</i>, was added at the very top of the building during the reign of <a href="/wiki/Domitian" title="Domitian">Domitian</a>. This comprised a gallery for the common poor, <a href="/wiki/Slavery" title="Slavery">slaves</a> and women. It would have been either standing room only, or would have had very steep wooden benches. Some groups were banned altogether from the Colosseum, notably gravediggers, actors and former gladiators.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Each tier was divided into sections (<i>maeniana</i>) by curved passages and low walls (<i>praecinctiones</i> or <i>baltei</i>), and were subdivided into <i>cunei</i>, or wedges, by the steps and aisles from the vomitoria. Each row (<i>gradus</i>) of seats was numbered, permitting each individual seat to be exactly designated by its gradus, cuneus, and number.<sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Arena_and_hypogeum">Arena and hypogeum</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:0_Colosseum_-_Rome_111001_(2).JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/0_Colosseum_-_Rome_111001_%282%29.JPG/250px-0_Colosseum_-_Rome_111001_%282%29.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/0_Colosseum_-_Rome_111001_%282%29.JPG/500px-0_Colosseum_-_Rome_111001_%282%29.JPG 2x" data-file-width="3610" data-file-height="2407"></a><figcaption>The Colosseum arena, showing the <i><a href="/wiki/Hypogeum" title="Hypogeum">hypogeum</a></i> now filled with walls. The walls were added early in the Colosseum's existence when it was decided it would no longer be flooded and used for naval battles.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The arena itself was 83 meters by 48 meters (272 ft by 157 ft / 280 by 163 Roman feet).<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It comprised a wooden floor covered by sand (the Latin word for sand is <i>harena</i> or <i>arena</i>), covering an elaborate underground structure called the <i><a href="/wiki/Hypogeum" title="Hypogeum">hypogeum</a></i> (literally meaning "underground"). The hypogeum was not part of the original construction but was ordered to be built by Emperor <a href="/wiki/Domitian" title="Domitian">Domitian</a>. Little now remains of the original arena floor, but the <i>hypogeum</i> is still clearly visible. It consisted of a two-level subterranean network of tunnels and cages beneath the arena where gladiators and animals were held before contests began. Eighty vertical shafts provided instant access to the arena for caged animals and scenery pieces concealed underneath; larger hinged platforms, called <i>hegmata</i>, provided access for elephants and the like. It was restructured on numerous occasions; at least twelve different phases of construction can be seen.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The <i>hypogeum</i> was connected by tunnels to a number of points outside the Colosseum. Animals and performers were brought through the tunnel from nearby stables, with the gladiators' barracks at the <a href="/wiki/Ludus_Magnus" title="Ludus Magnus">Ludus Magnus</a> to the east also being connected by tunnels. Separate tunnels were provided for the Emperor and the <a href="/wiki/Vestal_Virgins" class="mw-redirect" title="Vestal Virgins">Vestal Virgins</a> to permit them to enter and exit the Colosseum without needing to pass through the crowds.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Substantial quantities of machinery also existed in the <i>hypogeum</i>. Elevators and pulleys raised and lowered scenery and props, as well as lifting caged animals to the surface for release. There is evidence for the existence of major <a href="/wiki/Hydraulic" class="mw-redirect" title="Hydraulic">hydraulic</a> mechanisms<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and according to ancient accounts, it was possible to flood the arena rapidly, presumably via a connection to a nearby aqueduct. However, the construction of the hypogeum at Domitian's behest put an end to the practise of flooding, and thus also to naval battles, early in the Colosseum's existence. There is however wide debate over the practicality and logistics of this phenomenon which leads to speculation over its actuality. This is mostly because there is no physical evidence of naumachiae at the Colosseum remains.<sup id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Supporting_buildings">Supporting buildings</h3></div>
<p>The Colosseum and its activities supported a substantial industry in the area. In addition to the amphitheatre itself, many other buildings nearby were linked to the games. Immediately to the east is the remains of the <i><a href="/wiki/Ludus_Magnus" title="Ludus Magnus">Ludus Magnus</a></i>, a training school for gladiators. This was connected to the Colosseum by an underground passage, to allow easy access for the gladiators. The <i>Ludus Magnus</i> had its own miniature training arena, which was itself a popular attraction for Roman spectators. Other training schools were in the same area, including the <i>Ludus Matutinus</i> (Morning School), where fighters of animals were trained, plus the Dacian and Gallic Schools.
</p><p>Also nearby were the <i>Armamentarium</i>, comprising an armory to store weapons; the <i>Summum Choragium</i>, where machinery was stored; the <i>Sanitarium</i>, which had facilities to treat wounded gladiators; and the <i>Spoliarium</i>, where bodies of dead gladiators were stripped of their armor and disposed of.
</p><p>Around the perimeter of the Colosseum, at a distance of 18 m (59 ft) from the perimeter, was a series of tall stone posts, with five remaining on the eastern side. Various explanations have been advanced for their presence; they may have been a religious boundary, or an outer boundary for ticket checks, or an anchor for the <i><a href="/wiki/Velarium" title="Velarium">velarium</a></i> or awning.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The Commodus Passage, named after <a href="/wiki/Commodus" title="Commodus">Commodus</a>, was used by Roman emperors to enter the Colosseum discreetly. A failed assassination attempt against Commodus occurred in the passage. It was rediscovered in the 1810s. Restoration work which restored decorative stuccoes and added a walkway was conducted on the passage from October 2024 to September 2025. The passage will be opened to the public on 27 October 2025. Another restoration project is planned to begin in 2026.<sup id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Use">Use</h2></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ave_Caesar_Morituri_te_Salutant_(G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me)_01.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Ave_Caesar_Morituri_te_Salutant_%28G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me%29_01.jpg/250px-Ave_Caesar_Morituri_te_Salutant_%28G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me%29_01.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="157" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Ave_Caesar_Morituri_te_Salutant_%28G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me%29_01.jpg/500px-Ave_Caesar_Morituri_te_Salutant_%28G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me%29_01.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="1881"></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Ave_Imperator,_morituri_te_salutant" title="Ave Imperator, morituri te salutant">Ave Imperator, morituri te salutant</a> (Hail, <a href="/wiki/Caesar_(title)" title="Caesar (title)">Cesar</a>, those who will die salute you)</i>, by <a href="/wiki/Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me" title="Jean-Léon Gérôme">Jean-Léon Gérôme</a>, 1859</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Colosseum was used to host <a href="/wiki/Gladiator" title="Gladiator">gladiatorial</a> shows as well as a variety of other events. The shows, called <span title="Latin-language text"><i lang="la"><a href="/wiki/Munera_(ancient_Rome)" title="Munera (ancient Rome)">munera</a></i></span>, were always given by private individuals rather than the state. They had a strong religious element but were also demonstrations of power and family prestige and were immensely popular. Another major attraction was the animal hunt, or <i><a href="/wiki/Venatio" title="Venatio">venatio</a></i>. This utilized a great variety of wild beasts, mainly imported from Africa and the Middle East, and included creatures such as <a href="/wiki/Rhinoceros" title="Rhinoceros">rhinoceros</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hippopotamus" title="Hippopotamus">hippopotamuses</a>, <a href="/wiki/Elephant" title="Elephant">elephants</a>, <a href="/wiki/Giraffe" title="Giraffe">giraffes</a>, <a href="/wiki/Aurochs" title="Aurochs">aurochs</a>, <a href="/wiki/Wisent" class="mw-redirect" title="Wisent">wisents</a>, <a href="/wiki/Barbary_lion" title="Barbary lion">Barbary lions</a>, <a href="/wiki/Leopard" title="Leopard">panthers</a>, <a href="/wiki/Leopard" title="Leopard">leopards</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bears" class="mw-redirect" title="Bears">bears</a>, <a href="/wiki/Caspian_tiger" title="Caspian tiger">Caspian tigers</a>, <a href="/wiki/Crocodile" title="Crocodile">crocodiles</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ostrich" title="Ostrich">ostriches</a>. Battles and hunts were often staged amid elaborate sets with movable trees and buildings. These events could be huge in scale; <a href="/wiki/Trajan" title="Trajan">Trajan</a> is said to have celebrated his victories in <a href="/wiki/Dacia" title="Dacia">Dacia</a> in 107 with contests involving 11,000 animals and 10,000 gladiators over the course of 123 days. During lunch intervals, executions <i><a href="/wiki/Damnatio_ad_bestias" title="Damnatio ad bestias">ad bestias</a></i> would be staged. Those condemned to death would be sent into the arena, naked and unarmed, to face the beasts of death which would literally tear them to pieces. Acrobats and magicians would also perform, usually during the intervals.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Jean-Leon_Gerome_Pollice_Verso.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Jean-Leon_Gerome_Pollice_Verso.jpg/250px-Jean-Leon_Gerome_Pollice_Verso.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="168" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Jean-Leon_Gerome_Pollice_Verso.jpg/500px-Jean-Leon_Gerome_Pollice_Verso.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2425" data-file-height="1630"></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Pollice_Verso_(G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me)" title="Pollice Verso (Gérôme)">Pollice Verso</a></i> (<i>Thumbs Down</i>) by <a href="/wiki/Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me" title="Jean-Léon Gérôme">Jean-Léon Gérôme</a>, 1872</figcaption></figure>
<p>During the early days of the Colosseum, ancient writers recorded that the building was used for <i><a href="/wiki/Naumachia" title="Naumachia">naumachiae</a></i> (more properly known as <i>navalia proelia</i>) or simulated sea battles. Accounts of the inaugural games held by Titus in AD 80 describe it being filled with water for a display of specially trained swimming horses and bulls. There is also an account of a re-enactment of a famous sea battle between the <a href="/wiki/Corfu" title="Corfu">Corcyrean</a> (Corfiot) Greeks and the <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Corinth" title="Ancient Corinth">Corinthians</a>. This has been the subject of some debate among historians; although providing the water would not have been a problem, it is unclear how the arena could have been waterproofed, nor would there have been enough space in the arena for the warships to move around. It has been suggested that the reports either have the location wrong or that the Colosseum originally featured a wide floodable channel down its central axis (which would later have been replaced by the <a href="/wiki/Hypogeum" title="Hypogeum">hypogeum</a>).<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p><i>Sylvae</i> or recreations of natural scenes were also held in the arena. Painters, technicians and architects would construct a simulation of a forest with real trees and bushes planted in the arena's floor, and animals would then be introduced. Such scenes might be used simply to display a natural environment for the urban population, or could otherwise be used as the backdrop for hunts or dramas depicting episodes from mythology. They were also occasionally used for executions in which the hero of the story — played by a condemned person — was killed in one of various gruesome but mythologically authentic ways, such as being mauled by beasts or burned to death.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Modern_use">Modern use<span class="anchor" id="Today"></span></h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Rom_Colosseum_Sept_2021_3.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Rom_Colosseum_Sept_2021_3.jpg/250px-Rom_Colosseum_Sept_2021_3.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Rom_Colosseum_Sept_2021_3.jpg/500px-Rom_Colosseum_Sept_2021_3.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5464" data-file-height="3640"></a><figcaption>Aerial view of the Colosseum, 2021</figcaption></figure>
<p>Beneath the Colosseum, a network of subterranean passageways that were once used for transporting wild animals and gladiators to the arena, opened to the public in summer 2010.<sup id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The Colosseum is also the site of Roman Catholic ceremonies in the 20th and 21st centuries. For instance, <a href="/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XVI" title="Pope Benedict XVI">Pope Benedict XVI</a> led the <a href="/wiki/Stations_of_the_Cross" title="Stations of the Cross">Stations of the Cross</a> called the <a href="/wiki/Scriptural_Way_of_the_Cross" title="Scriptural Way of the Cross">Scriptural Way of the Cross</a> (which calls for more meditation) at the Colosseum<sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> on <a href="/wiki/Good_Friday" title="Good Friday">Good Fridays</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-wayofthecross-frommers_8-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wayofthecross-frommers-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Restoration">Restoration</h4></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Colosseum_under_renovation_in_Rome,_Italy_(Ank_Kumar)_03.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Colosseum_under_renovation_in_Rome%2C_Italy_%28Ank_Kumar%29_03.jpg/250px-Colosseum_under_renovation_in_Rome%2C_Italy_%28Ank_Kumar%29_03.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Colosseum_under_renovation_in_Rome%2C_Italy_%28Ank_Kumar%29_03.jpg/500px-Colosseum_under_renovation_in_Rome%2C_Italy_%28Ank_Kumar%29_03.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5570" data-file-height="3713"></a><figcaption>Colosseum under renovation, 2015</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 2011, <a href="/wiki/Diego_Della_Valle" title="Diego Della Valle">Diego Della Valle</a>, head of the shoe firm <a href="/wiki/Tod%27s" title="Tod's">Tod's</a>, entered into an agreement with local officials to sponsor a €25 million restoration of the Colosseum. Work was planned to begin at the end of 2011, taking up to two and a half years.<sup id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Due to the controversial nature of using a <a href="/wiki/Public%E2%80%93private_partnership" title="Public–private partnership">public–private partnership</a> to fund the restoration, work was delayed and began in 2013. The restoration is the first full cleaning and repair in the Colosseum's history.<sup id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The first stage is to clean and restore the Colosseum's arcaded façade and replace the metal enclosures that block the ground-level arches. After three years, the work was completed on 1 July 2016, when the Italian minister of culture, Dario Franceschini, also announced that the funds have been committed to replace the floors by the end of 2018. These will provide a stage that Franceschini says will be used for "cultural events of the highest level."<sup id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The project also includes creating a services center and restoring the galleries and underground spaces inside the Colosseum.<sup id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Since 1 November 2017, the top two levels have been opened for guided visits. The fourth level held the marketplace, and the top fifth tier is where the poorest citizens, the plebeians, gathered and watched the show, bringing picnics for the day-long event.<sup id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Significance_in_Christianity">Significance in Christianity</h2></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Christian_Martyrs%27_Last_Prayer_GA%26C.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/The_Christian_Martyrs%27_Last_Prayer_GA%26C.jpg/250px-The_Christian_Martyrs%27_Last_Prayer_GA%26C.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/The_Christian_Martyrs%27_Last_Prayer_GA%26C.jpg/500px-The_Christian_Martyrs%27_Last_Prayer_GA%26C.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6530" data-file-height="3810"></a><figcaption><i>The Christian Martyrs' Last Prayer</i>, by <a href="/wiki/Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me" title="Jean-Léon Gérôme">Jean-Léon Gérôme</a> (1883)</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Colosseum is generally regarded by Christians as a site of the martyrdom of large numbers of believers during the <a href="/wiki/Persecution_of_Christians_in_the_Roman_Empire" title="Persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire">persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire</a>, as evidenced by Church history and tradition.<sup id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-newadvent.org_49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-newadvent.org-49"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On the other hand, other scholars believe that the majority of martyrdoms may have occurred at other venues within the city of Rome, rather than at the Colosseum, citing a lack of still-intact physical evidence or historical records.<sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Brockman2011_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brockman2011-52"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> These scholars assert that "some Christians were executed as common criminals in the Colosseum—their crime being refusal to reverence the Roman gods", but most <a href="/wiki/Christian_martyr" title="Christian martyr">Christian martyrs</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Early_Church" class="mw-redirect" title="Early Church">early Church</a> were executed for their faith at the <a href="/wiki/Circus_Maximus" title="Circus Maximus">Circus Maximus</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Brockman_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brockman-54"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Potter1999_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Potter1999-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> According to <a href="/wiki/Irenaeus" title="Irenaeus">Irenaeus</a> (died about 202), <a href="/wiki/Ignatius_of_Antioch" title="Ignatius of Antioch">Ignatius of Antioch</a> was fed to the lions in Rome around 107 A.D. and although Irenaeus says nothing about this happening at the Colosseum, tradition ascribes it to that place.<sup id="cite_ref-Litfin2007_56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Litfin2007-56"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Flinn2006_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Flinn2006-57"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Norbert_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Norbert-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Christoffer_Wilhelm_Eckersberg_-_View_of_the_interior_of_the_Colosseum_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Christoffer_Wilhelm_Eckersberg_-_View_of_the_interior_of_the_Colosseum_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-Christoffer_Wilhelm_Eckersberg_-_View_of_the_interior_of_the_Colosseum_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="284" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Christoffer_Wilhelm_Eckersberg_-_View_of_the_interior_of_the_Colosseum_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/500px-Christoffer_Wilhelm_Eckersberg_-_View_of_the_interior_of_the_Colosseum_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2509" data-file-height="2848"></a><figcaption><i>View of the interior of the Colosseum</i>, by <a href="/wiki/Christoffer_Wilhelm_Eckersberg" title="Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg">C. W. Eckersberg</a> (1815)</figcaption></figure>
<p>In the Middle Ages, the Colosseum was not regarded as a monument, and was used as what some modern sources label a "quarry,"<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> which is to say that stones from the Colosseum were taken for the building of other sacred sites.<sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This fact is used to support the idea that, at a time when sites associated with martyrs were highly venerated the Colosseum was not being treated as a sacred site.<sup id="cite_ref-New_Advent_62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-New_Advent-62"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It was not included in the itineraries compiled for the use of pilgrims nor in works such as the 12th century <i><a href="/wiki/Mirabilia_Urbis_Romae" title="Mirabilia Urbis Romae">Mirabilia Urbis Romae</a></i> ("Marvels of the City of Rome"), which claims the <a href="/wiki/Circus_Flaminius" title="Circus Flaminius">Circus Flaminius</a> – but not the Colosseum – as the site of martyrdoms.<sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Part of the structure was inhabited by a <a href="/wiki/Religious_order#Christian_tradition" title="Religious order">Christian religious order</a>, but it is not known whether this was for any particular religious reason.
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Pope_Pius_V" title="Pope Pius V">Pope Pius V</a> (1566–1572) is said to have recommended that pilgrims gather sand from the arena of the Colosseum to serve as a relic, on the grounds that it was impregnated with the blood of martyrs, although some of his contemporaries did not share his conviction.<sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A century later Fioravante Martinelli listed the Colosseum at the head of a list of places sacred to the martyrs in his 1653 book <i>Roma ex ethnica sacra</i>. Martinelli's book evidently had an effect on public opinion; in response to Cardinal Altieri's proposal some years later to turn the Colosseum into a bullring, Carlo Tomassi published a pamphlet in protest against what he regarded as an act of desecration. The ensuing controversy persuaded <a href="/wiki/Pope_Clement_X" title="Pope Clement X">Pope Clement X</a> to close the Colosseum's external arcades and declare it a sanctuary.<sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Cruz_del_Jubileo_2000_en_el_Coliseo_-_detalle.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Cruz_del_Jubileo_2000_en_el_Coliseo_-_detalle.JPG/250px-Cruz_del_Jubileo_2000_en_el_Coliseo_-_detalle.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Cruz_del_Jubileo_2000_en_el_Coliseo_-_detalle.JPG/500px-Cruz_del_Jubileo_2000_en_el_Coliseo_-_detalle.JPG 2x" data-file-width="3872" data-file-height="2592"></a><figcaption>Cross dedicated to the Christian martyrs, placed in 2000 by <a href="/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II" title="Pope John Paul II">Pope John Paul II</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>At the insistence of St. <a href="/wiki/Leonard_of_Port_Maurice" title="Leonard of Port Maurice">Leonard of Port Maurice</a>, Pope <a href="/wiki/Benedict_XIV" class="mw-redirect" title="Benedict XIV">Benedict XIV</a> (1740–1758) forbade the quarrying of the Colosseum and erected <a href="/wiki/Stations_of_the_Cross" title="Stations of the Cross">Stations of the Cross</a> around the arena, which remained until February 1874.<sup id="cite_ref-Benedict_66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Benedict-66"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Benedict_Joseph_Labre" title="Benedict Joseph Labre">Benedict Joseph Labre</a> spent the later years of his life within the walls of the Colosseum, living on <a href="/wiki/Alms" title="Alms">alms</a>, before he died in 1783.<sup id="cite_ref-Benedict_66-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Benedict-66"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Several 19th century popes funded repair and restoration work on the Colosseum, and it still retains its Christian connection today. A <a href="/wiki/Christian_cross" title="Christian cross">Christian cross</a> stands in the Colosseum, with a plaque, stating:
</p>
<blockquote><p>The amphitheater, one consecrated to triumphs, entertainments, and the impious worship of pagan gods, is now dedicated to the sufferings of the martyrs purified from impious superstitions.<sup id="cite_ref-Litfin2007_56-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Litfin2007-56"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>Other Christian crosses stand in several points around the arena and every <a href="/wiki/Good_Friday" title="Good Friday">Good Friday</a> the Pope leads a <a href="/wiki/Via_Crucis" class="mw-redirect" title="Via Crucis">Via Crucis</a> procession to the amphitheater.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Flora">Flora</h2></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Weed_Whacking_the_Colosseum_(2883935844).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Weed_Whacking_the_Colosseum_%282883935844%29.jpg/250px-Weed_Whacking_the_Colosseum_%282883935844%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="222" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Weed_Whacking_the_Colosseum_%282883935844%29.jpg/500px-Weed_Whacking_the_Colosseum_%282883935844%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2792" data-file-height="2477"></a><figcaption>Weed control</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Colosseum has a wide and well-documented history of <a href="/wiki/Flora_(plants)" class="mw-redirect" title="Flora (plants)">flora</a> ever since <a href="/wiki/Domenico_Panaroli" title="Domenico Panaroli">Domenico Panaroli</a> made the first catalogue of its plants in 1643. Since then, 684 species have been identified there. The peak was in 1855 (420 species). Attempts were made in 1871 to eradicate the vegetation, because of concerns over the damage that was being caused to the masonry, but much of it has returned.<sup id="cite_ref-claridge_18-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-claridge-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Two hundred forty-two species have been counted today and of the species first identified by Panaroli, 200 remain.
</p><p>The variation of plants can be explained by the change of climate in Rome through the centuries, as well as by <a href="/wiki/Bird_migration" title="Bird migration">bird migration</a>, flower blooming, and the growth of Rome that caused the Colosseum to become embedded within the modern city centre rather than on the outskirts of the ancient city. Deliberate import of animal species is another contributing cause, as seeds were unwittingly carried either on the fur or in the feces of animals brought there from all corners of the empire.<sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="In_popular_culture">In popular culture</h2></div>
<p>The Colosseum has appeared in numerous films, artworks and games. It is featured in films such as <i><a href="/wiki/Roman_Holiday" title="Roman Holiday">Roman Holiday</a></i>,<sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/Gladiator_(2000_film)" title="Gladiator (2000 film)">Gladiator</a></i>,<sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/The_Way_of_the_Dragon" title="The Way of the Dragon">The Way of the Dragon</a></i>,<sup id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <i><a href="/wiki/Jumper_(2008_film)" title="Jumper (2008 film)">Jumper</a></i>,<sup id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <i><a href="/wiki/Godzilla_x_Kong:_The_New_Empire" title="Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire">Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-72"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Additionally, <a href="/wiki/Coliseum_Mountain" title="Coliseum Mountain">Coliseum Mountain</a> in <a href="/wiki/Alberta" title="Alberta">Alberta</a>, <a href="/wiki/Canada" title="Canada">Canada</a> was named after the Colosseum.
</p><p>Several architectural works have also been modelled on or inspired by, the Colosseum. These include:
</p>
<ul><li>The <i>Kongresshalle</i>, or "Congress Hall", (1935, unfinished) at the <a href="/wiki/Nazi_Party_Rally_grounds" class="mw-redirect" title="Nazi Party Rally grounds">Nazi Party Rally grounds</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nuremberg" title="Nuremberg">Nuremberg</a>, <a href="/wiki/Germany" title="Germany">Germany</a></li>
<li>The <a href="/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games" title="Summer Olympic Games">Summer Olympic Games</a> <a href="/wiki/Olympic_medal" title="Olympic medal">medal</a> from 1928 to 2000, designed by <a href="/wiki/Giuseppe_Cassioli" title="Giuseppe Cassioli">Giuseppe Cassioli</a>, features a depiction of the Colosseum. At the <a href="/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics" title="2004 Summer Olympics">2004 Summer Olympics</a> in <a href="/wiki/Athens" title="Athens">Athens</a> the Colosseum was replaced by a depiction of the <a href="/wiki/Panathinaiko_Stadium" class="mw-redirect" title="Panathinaiko Stadium">Panathinaiko Stadium</a></li>
<li>The exterior of the <a href="/wiki/Vancouver_Public_Library" title="Vancouver Public Library">Vancouver Public Library</a> in <a href="/wiki/British_Columbia" title="British Columbia">British Columbia</a> resembles the current state of the Colosseum. It was designed by <a href="/wiki/Moshe_Safdie" title="Moshe Safdie">Moshe Safdie</a>.</li>
<li>The <a href="/wiki/Los_Angeles_Memorial_Coliseum" title="Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum">Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum</a> entrance was inspired by the Colosseum.</li>
<li>The <a href="/wiki/Palazzo_della_Civilt%C3%A0_Italiana" title="Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana">Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana</a> was very closely modelled on the Colosseum. It was built for Mussolini for the Universal Exhibition of 1942 but the exhibition never happened due to the outbreak of World War II. The architects were Giovanni Guerrini, Ernesto Bruno La Padula, and Mario Romano.</li>
<li><a href="/wiki/McCaig%27s_Tower" title="McCaig's Tower">McCaig's Tower</a>, overlooking <a href="/wiki/Oban" title="Oban">Oban</a>, Scotland.</li>
<li><a href="/wiki/Nero_Burning_ROM" title="Nero Burning ROM">Nero Burning ROM</a>'s logo is inspired by the colosseum.</li></ul>
